title: Aqueous zinc-iodine batteries achieve 60,000 charge cycles
content: Flinders University researchers have developed a high-performing, safe, and sustainable aqueous zinc-iodine rechargeable battery (AZIB) as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) for large-scale energy storage.Interestingly, it retains 60,000 charge-discharge cycles and charges in three minutes. “Rechargeable aqueous zinc-iodine batteries are shaping up as a viable alternative to lithium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage, and our group is now working with industry to establish a prototyping platform for this battery system,” said Zhongfan Jia, Associate Professor in Chemistry, Matthew Flinders Fellow at Flinders University’s College of Science and Engineering.The shuttle effect fixLithium-ion batteries dominate electric vehicles and portable tech, but come with a heavy toll. These batteries are expensive, prone to fire risks, and produce massive environmental waste. Australia alone generates roughly 3,300 tonnes of lithium battery waste annually, a figure projected to skyrocket past 136,000 tonnes by 2036. Zinc-iodine alternatives offered a water-based, non-flammable escape route. But the face the “shuttle effect,” where polyiodine species leak through the battery separator and degrade performance over time. That is where starch changes the game.The team solved this by creating a host material using a low-cost, biodegradable cyclodextrin-based polymer (derived from starch) that traps and releases polyhalides.Cyclodextrin molecules are widely used in cosmetics and food. The Flinders team engineered a microscopic cage. Its hydrophilic exterior and hydrophobic interior trap and release polyhalides on demand, stopping the leakage cold.“This system offers a new approach to mitigate polyiodide shuttling by using polymers derived from inexpensive, biodegradable oligosaccharides, thereby enabling sustainable and long-lasting aqueous zinc-iodine batteries,” said Associate Professor Zhongfan Jia, lead researcher on the project.The performance stats read like a wishlist for large-scale grid storage. Operating at 1.3 to 1.4 volts, the battery delivers a capacity of 200 mAh/g over 8,000 cycles when fully charged in seven minutes. Drop the target capacity slightly to 150 mAh/g, and a ultra-fast three-minute charge yields over 60,000 cycles.As per the study, the battery degrades at an almost imperceptible rate of 0.0001% to 0.0003% per cycle, explaining how it achieves over 60,000 cycles. Australia’s zinc advantageZinc-based batteries offer a far safer, cost-effective, and highly accessible alternative to lithium-ion systems without sacrificing performance. These batteries eliminate fire risks while matching or exceeding lithium-ion in both specific energy and energy density. Their low cost and abundant raw materials have made them the dominant global standard for single-use energy storage.Lithium processing is currently heavily concentrated in China, leaving countries vulnerable to supply shocks. The discovery carries major economic implications for Australia. While the nation struggles with lithium processing, it sits on major known zinc reserves.AZIBs typically rely on zinc metal as an anode, giving Australia a significant strategic advantage in the transition to next-generation energy storage. The nation holds between 20 percent and 28 percent of the world’s total known zinc reserves.First co-author Shangxu Jiang notes that leveraging these vast domestic resources could anchor a safer, sovereign energy storage industryThe Flinders lab is now working directly with industry partners to build a commercial prototyping platform. Hence, it looks like the next green energy transition might not be powered by scarce, fiery metals, but by zinc and ordinary plant sugar.The findings were published in the journal Angewandte Chemie.

title: Australia taps US firm for 10,000-ton AUKUS nuclear submarines
content: Australia has selected a joint venture involving U.S. engineering firm Amentum and Laing O’Rourke to help deliver a major new shipyard for its future nuclear-powered submarine fleet.Australian Naval Infrastructure named the partnership as its Capability Partner for the construction yard at Osborne, near Adelaide in South Australia.The site will eventually build Australia’s SSN-AUKUS submarines under the security partnership involving Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. For Washington, the project represents another major step in turning AUKUS from a strategic agreement into physical industrial capacity.Building Australia’s nuclear yardAmentum and Laing O’Rourke will work inside ANI’s Integrated Delivery Office under a long-term arrangement. Their team will help manage the nuclear-related elements of the program. They will also oversee construction activities and provide safety leadership.The partners will coordinate work packages and support engagement with contractors across the expanding project. A major challenge will involve managing interfaces between nuclear and conventional construction areas.That work matters because the Osborne facility will become Australia’s first dedicated construction site for conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines. The yard will need specialized infrastructure for submarine assembly, outfitting, testing and commissioning.Amentum brings decades of experience from nuclear submarine programs. The company said its background includes nuclear licensing and work alongside independent regulators.Mark Whitney, president of Amentum Energy & Environment, described the project as a defining opportunity for Australia’s nuclear future. “Amentum has the opportunity to be part of a once-in-a-generation national endeavor,” Whitney said. He added that the effort could shape Australia’s nuclear capability for decades.Kim Katheklakis, Amentum Australia’s managing director, said the team will provide practical leadership throughout project delivery. Its responsibilities will include governance, logistics, commissioning and digital engineering. Supply-chain quality will also form a major part of the effort.AUKUS moves into constructionThe Osborne yard represents one of the most ambitious industrial projects within the broader AUKUS submarine effort. Australia plans to operate nuclear-powered submarines for the first time through the partnership. The future SSN-AUKUS fleet will give Australia a nuclear-powered submarine capability without nuclear weapons.That distinction remains central to the country’s submarine strategy. The United States will play a critical role in Australia’s transition toward nuclear-powered naval operations. Australia plans to build SSN-AUKUS submarines expected to displace around 10,000 tons, giving the country a far larger and more capable undersea platform than its current conventionally powered fleet.American industry and government agencies have already supported workforce development and submarine technology efforts under AUKUS. The new Australian shipyard could eventually become another important industrial node supporting allied submarine operations across the Indo-Pacific.Developing that capacity will require far more than constructing buildings. Australia must establish a skilled workforce capable of supporting nuclear submarine construction over several decades. It must also develop specialized supply chains and regulatory expertise.Amentum and Laing O’Rourke will therefore join a project extending beyond conventional shipyard construction. The partners will help establish the systems needed to manage one of Australia’s most technically demanding defense programs.Industrial betAustralia expects the broader AUKUS effort to create thousands of skilled jobs in South Australia. Osborne already serves as a major center for Australian naval construction. The new submarine yard will significantly expand its role.For the United States, a successful Australian submarine industry could strengthen allied capacity in a strategically important region. It could also deepen industrial links among the three AUKUS partners.The project now moves into a phase where engineering, construction and workforce development will carry as much importance as diplomacy.Australia has committed to building a sovereign nuclear-powered submarine capability. Amentum and Laing O’Rourke now have a role in creating the industrial foundation needed to make that goal possible.

title: China tests 800-seat flying wing aircraft bigger than the B-2 bomber
content: China is exploring a radical passenger aircraft design that could carry more than 800 people, potentially creating one of the largest airliners ever conceived.The aircraft abandons the familiar tube-and-wing layout used by Boeing and Airbus. Instead, nearly the entire structure forms a broad flying wing that generates lift.Researchers at the China Aerodynamics Research and Development Center, or CARDC, have already begun testing a scale model. Their work examines the aerodynamic behavior of an exceptionally large flying-wing configuration.At 85 meters wide, the proposed aircraft would have a wingspan roughly 1.6 times greater than the B-2 Spirit. The aircraft would measure 43 meters from front to back.That size puts the concept in a different category from today’s commercial aircraft. Airbus A380 configurations typically seat about 555 passengers, well below the Chinese design’s proposed capacity. The researchers have not announced plans for a full-scale prototype. For now, the project serves as a research platform for studying future large passenger aircraft.Giant wing targets efficiencyFlying-wing aircraft combine the fuselage and wings into a single lifting structure. That approach can reduce aerodynamic drag and increase the amount of lift generated across the aircraft.Li Yonghong and his research team believe the configuration offers major aerodynamic advantages. Higher lift-to-drag ratios could support longer flights and lower energy consumption. The proposed aircraft has a reference wing area of about 1,395 square meters. Its leading edge sweeps back 37 degrees, with a 28-degree sweep along the trailing edge.The design targets a cruise speed of Mach 0.8, similar to many modern widebody passenger jets. CARDC initially developed the concept around a 250-seat aircraft. Researchers later scaled the configuration toward the 800-passenger category.Wind tunnel puts design CARDC built a stainless-steel model at a scale of 1:52 to investigate the concept. The model measures roughly 0.8 meters long and has a wingspan of 1.6 meters.Engineers tested it inside the institute’s 2.4-meter transonic wind tunnel. Test speeds ranged from Mach 0.4 to Mach 0.8. The team studied aerodynamic performance, airflow transitions, stability and structural deformation. Researchers also examined measurement techniques for slender flying-wing shapes.The model achieved a maximum lift-to-drag ratio of about 20 below Mach 0.7. At its target cruise speed of Mach 0.8, that figure dropped to 17.6. Those results give researchers a benchmark for studying similar aircraft configurations. They could also help engineers improve computational models and wind-tunnel testing methods.China eyes bigger aircraftThe flying-wing research adds another branch to China’s large-aircraft ambitions. CARDC has contributed to projects including the C919 passenger jet and Y-20 military transport.China also continues work on the C929, a planned 280-seat long-range widebody. Officials expect its first flight around 2030. The country has separately explored the C949, a proposed supersonic passenger aircraft. That project has attracted comparisons with NASA’s X-59 research.For American aerospace observers, the flying-wing project presents an unusual civilian application for a configuration associated with the B-2 bomber. Turning that shape into an 800-passenger airliner would create major engineering challenges.

title: China tests humanoids with real household chores in major robot games
content: Humanoid robots are being tested in places that look less like sporting arenas and more like workplaces and homes, as China’s robot competitions put machines through hotel, library, and household tasks.The scenario-based events are part of the second World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG), offering a test of how robots handle practical work in less standardized environments. Robots were scored out of 300 points for three tasks: tidying a living room, folding clothes in a bedroom, and washing and hanging laundry in a bathroom and on a balcony. An unexpected parcel-delivery task required robots to respond to a voice command, bring a package indoors, and then resume their previous chores.Humanoid robots face the messiness of real lifeThe scoring system was designed to penalize mistakes that could matter in a real household. Robots lost points for collisions, dropped objects, and crossing boundaries. If a human intervened during a run, the attempt was treated as remote-controlled, and the scoring weight was reduced to 0.5, according to the report.TianYi 2.0, developed by Beijing-based humanoid robot maker X-Humanoid, is competing in the scenario events. The wheeled robot can adjust its torso height between 130 and 165 centimeters and operate for more than two hours on a charge, Global Times (GT) reported. The company said its robots use the Huisi Kaiwu operation platform, with conventional competitions focused on being “higher and faster” and scenario events aimed at being “better at working.”The practical testing began Sunday with a hotel-service competition at the Beijing Continental Grand Hotel. Robots had 30 minutes to transport guests’ luggage to assigned rooms, replenish towels, slippers and bottled water, remove used linen and make beds.Simply completing the assigned tasks within the time limit was not enough for a high score. Neatness was also assessed, while autonomous operation received a higher weighting than teleoperation. The real buildings present machines with challenges including unstructured spaces, deformable soft goods, difficult-to-balance loaded trolleys and long sequences of tasks that can expose instability.Analysts highlighted another practical obstacle: narrow hotel corridors and maneuvering luggage through those confined spaces tested a robot’s ability to operate in limited space. A separate library-shelving competition also took place Sunday. Robots operating inside a working library had 30 minutes to collect returned books, shelve them and correct misplaced volumes. The WHRG said the challenge tested precision, visual recognition and reasoning.The real test is autonomyThe games also include six events based in real-world settings and eight dexterous-hand “micro-manipulation” contests, including tasks such as picking up beans and driving screws. AGILINK, spun off from Chinese humanoid robot maker AgiBot in January, says winning the dexterous-hand competition demonstrates a product’s capability and indicates it has passed a “demonstration-grade” threshold for real-world use, as reported by GT . According to experts, moving robots from standardized courses into hotels and homes tests the combined performance of their mechanical components, algorithms, and ability to adapt to specific scenarios. Autonomy is an important direction for the sector, because teleoperation still requires another person to operate or assist the robot.The second WHRG is scheduled for August 22–26 at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval. The event has attracted 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries, while the World Robot Conference is also scheduled to open in Beijing this week, putting several aspects of the country’s robotics development on display at the same time.

title: China's new humanoid robot can mirror human movements remotely
content: A Chinese firm is set to unveil a special-purpose humanoid robot, designed for reconnaissance, patrols, and operations in hazardous environments. The Fuxi robot, developed by China North Industries Group Corporation (NORINCO Group), can operate in all weather conditions and allows human operators to control its movements in real time remotely. Developed alongside a dedicated teleoperation system, Fuxi is intended to enable closer coordination between humans and robots during on-site missions. Recently, twenty-three humanoid robot teams tackled a real-world firefighting and rescue challenge in Beijing, testing their ability to perform practical tasks under unpredictable conditions.Humanoid robot patrolsThe full-size humanoid, developed by NORINCO’s innovation institute, uses domestically developed technologies focused on human motion sensing, motion transfer between robotic platforms, and whole-body coordination. Though further details have not been disclosed, the robot can identify personnel and issue alerts when it detects abnormal situations, supporting its use in sentry and surveillance roles, the Global Times (GT) reports.Fuxi is also designed for all-weather reconnaissance, intelligent patrols and operations in dangerous areas where direct human involvement could be difficult. Multiple robots can operate together in formations, while an individual robot can reproduce an operator’s movements in real time during remote-controlled missions.NORINCO has developed a dedicated teleoperation system called “external avatar” to support these capabilities. The company describes it as China’s first independently controllable teleoperation solution for full-size humanoid robots weighing around 198 pounds (90 kilograms).The system incorporates technologies for real-time human-motion remapping and remote control. It is intended for complex and high-risk environments and can support remote reconnaissance, unmanned operations, and specialized response missions. NORINCO said combining human control from a remote location with robots carrying out tasks on site could provide a new approach to unmanned operations in special-purpose scenarios, reports GT.A group of Fuxi robots will also demonstrate nighttime urban inspection operations during the event. The demonstration will highlight coordinated management among multiple robots, intelligent assessment and closed-loop responses, according to the company.Humanoids face realityChina’s humanoid robot industry is shifting its focus from flashy demonstrations to practical applications as manufacturers face growing pressure to prove the technology can deliver measurable economic value.More than 300 companies are expected at the World Robot Conference in Beijing this week, showcasing over 2,000 exhibits and more than 150 new products. The event comes as Chinese humanoid makers increasingly emphasize industrial inspection, material handling and other tasks rather than entertainment-focused demonstrations.The industry is also using the World Humanoid Robot Games, which begin in Beijing on August 22, to test robots in more demanding work scenarios. Competitions will include factory, hotel and household tasks such as packing, warehousing, industrial assembly, material feeding, retail services, EV charging and connecting cables. These applications require robots to do more than perform programmed movements. Machines must recognize unfamiliar objects, manipulate them repeatedly, recover from errors, and complete tasks without constant intervention from engineers, reports Reuters.The economic challenge remains significant. Robotics analysts estimate that 50 percent to 70 percent of humanoid robots produced this year could be used primarily to collect training data rather than perform paid work. Guotai Securities estimates an industrial humanoid would need to cost about 160,000 yuan ($22,300), including maintenance, to achieve payback within two years against a worker earning 80,000 yuan ($11,100) annually. However, robots currently typically cost between 300,000 and 500,000 yuan ($41,800-$69,600).According to experts, the challenge extends beyond hardware. Companies must also address shortages of skilled operators and the costs associated with transporting, deploying and maintaining humanoids. Together, these factors could determine whether China’s rapidly expanding humanoid sector moves from impressive prototypes to commercially viable robotic workers, reports Reuters.

title: E-2D Hawkeye upgrade aims to sharpen tracking of 3,000+ targets
content: The E-2D Advanced Hawkeye is moving toward a major technology upgrade that will improve how crews detect threats, manage information and operate the aircraft. Northrop Grumman has completed a government-led critical design review for the aircraft’s Block II upgrade, clearing the program to begin integration and testing.The company plans to start that work immediately, with upgraded E-2D aircraft scheduled for delivery by the end of the decade. The Block II effort is described as the largest upgrade to the platform since its development.The upgrade focuses on the aircraft’s mission systems, combining new hardware and software to improve situational awareness and reduce the workload on its crew. The goal is also to keep the aircraft adaptable as threats and military requirements change.The work is being built around a modular open systems approach, allowing newer technologies to be incorporated without requiring a complete redesign of the aircraft. The approach is intended to make future upgrades easier while supporting the long-term operation of the Navy’s E-2D fleet.Modular systems extend aircraft lifeA key part of the modernization is the use of commercial off-the-shelf technology. Using widely available components can help reduce costs and give the program more flexibility as new technologies become available.The Block II upgrade will also be incorporated directly into the E-2D production line. That means newly built aircraft can receive the upgraded systems during production, while aircraft already in service can be retrofitted. Expanding both production and retrofit capacity is intended to help modernize more aircraft over time.“Completing the Block II critical design review reflects the dedication and expertise of our team and partners. This upgrade strengthens the E-2D’s suite of capabilities, enhancing situational awareness, reducing crew workload and paving the way for future technology. We are continuing to deliver unmatched capability at speed to the U.S. Navy and our international partners.”The E-2D serves as an airborne early warning and command-and-control platform. Operating from the air, it is designed to help military forces detect and track activity and maintain a broader picture of what is happening around them.More capability, fewer disruptionsThe modernization is aimed not only at adding new capabilities but also at keeping the aircraft relevant for years to come. Its modular architecture is intended to make future technology insertions less disruptive, reducing the need for major overhauls each time a new capability is required.Northrop Grumman will apply the Block II configuration to both new aircraft and the existing fleet. This creates a path for older E-2Ds to receive the same modernization rather than relying solely on newly produced aircraft to bring the fleet up to date.The broader E-2D program supports more than 4,000 jobs at 411 companies across 40 US states, according to Northrop Grumman. The Block II upgrade therefore represents both a technology refresh for an existing aircraft and an effort to maintain the platform as a long-term part of the US defense fleet.

title: IBM's new modular cryogenic system for fault-tolerant quantum computer
content: Computing major IBM has unveiled its first modular cryogenic quantum fridge, which can be joined to create a single cooled environment that can handle hundreds of quantum chips. The cryogenic system, capable of cooling below 15 milliKelvin, is an important milestone as IBM works to release its large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. Quantum computers are regarded as the next frontier of computing, promising large-scale computations in a fraction of the time needed by the fastest supercomputers today. Unlike silicon-based computers that use binary bits, which can store only 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, which can store multiple values between 0 and 1 and carry out computations in parallel, exponentially increasing their computing power. Quantum bits, or qubits, usually work at extremely low temperatures, near absolute zero. Achieving this is a challenge but one that researchers have perfected using multi-stage devices called dilution refrigerators. The qubits operate inside chambers where temperatures are ultra-low, but the complex architecture of refrigeration and computing infrastructure make it difficult to build large-scale quantum computers. How IBM is solving this problemIBM has made a major design change to its existing cryogenic systems by moving to a rectangular form factor. The change is meant to enable denser integration of readout and control wiring and simplify coupling between adjacent cells, giving more room for quantum processors. The design change is also intended to separate components and subsystems so that they can be independently optimized in the future, even as the density of wiring, refrigeration, and quantum devices increases. In a recent demonstration, IBM combined two operational modules of its new cryogenic quantum refrigeration systems and showed how they could join forces to cool down to 4 Kelvin in under five days and final temperature of below 15 milliKelvin soon after. These are temperatures 180 times colder than deep space, and the module still delivers 12 times more wiring space than previous iterations of IBM’s systems, facilitating more chip-to-chip connections, within and outside the modules. Fault-tolerant quantum computerStanding more than eight feet (2.4 m) tall and eight feet wide, these modules also use IBM’s L-coupler technology to link directly with the quantum processors. The technology allows multiple quantum chips to communicate, share information and operate together as part of a larger quantum computer. The L-coupler technology is key in IBM’s quantum roadmap as it looks to build a larger quantum computer with at least a 1,000 programmable qubits by 2027. Working towards this goal, IBM will install its NightHawk quantum processors into these new cryogenic modules later this year and begin operational testing. For its plan to release a large-scale quantum computer by 2029, IBM intends to house thousands of qubits in each of these cryogenic modules. “Bringing fault-tolerant quantum computers to industries depends on several fundamental advances,” said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research in a press release shared with Interesting Engineering. “The successful connection and operation of these cryogenic modules signals a leap forward in that direction and will accelerate our progress alongside continued innovation in quantum hardware, software, and algorithms.”In addition to hardware, IBM is also focused on software required for a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Last year, it released a new error correction code that reduces the physical resources needed to achieve fault tolerance, the press release added.

title: New hydrogen turbine faces 72-hour test as US company eyes 1MW unit
content: A US hydrogen energy company has recently launched independent testing of its HOG hydrogen power turbine in order to verify its performance and advance it to one megawatt (MW).Vivify Technology’s validation program will focus on the 65-kilowatt (kW) nominal turbine test unit. The Florida energy and infrastructure firm said the system, HOG, serves as the technical basis for the containerized Flying Pig power platform and its planned larger commercial systems.Jason Herring, Vivify Technology’s founder and CEO, said the firm does not expect people to accept HOG’s performance claims without a proof. “We are putting the entire system under independent measurement, and we will publish the results.”The program is designed to independently measure how the complete hydrogen system performs. The results are set to be made public by the end of the year.Putting HOG to the testThe HOG (Hydrogen Oxygen Generator) is a hydrogen-based power system that uses water (including dirty and salt water) as its main input to produce electricity directly on site for facilities looking to reduce their reliance on the grid. It is also an emissions-free, self-supporting, closed-loop system.It generates hydrogen and demand, and combines the firm’s proprietary Pulsar system, multi-stage turbines, transformers, an H2O input generator, as well as combustion chambers. The generated hydrogen is then used in the system to produce electricity and heat.The firm announced an independent validation program for its hydrogen system.Credit: Vivify TechnologyThe company’s newest Flying Pig containerized system is based on the HOG. Each Flying Pig module is designed to provide about one megawatt (MW) of power. It incorporates micro-hydro and steam turbines, eight Pulsar units, water handling, transformers and other equipment. Vivify said that the independent validation of HOG will examine five areas, such as energy balance and efficiency, sustained electricity generation and power quality, hydrogen production and water use, emissions, and safety. The tests will measure the complete system rather than the turbine or another individual component. Targeting megawatt powerThe data should reveal how much energy the HOG uses and how much electricity it generates. The program will also include hydrogen-flow verification, water mass measurements, continuous monitoring and thermal inspections. An independent physics review and witnessed testing are also planned.The framework requires at least 72 hours of continuous operation. Meanwhile, the firm prefers 30 days of monitoring. The testing framework follows standards from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO).The initial tests will evaluate the 65 kW turbine configuration behind the Flying Pig system. The system is designed to reach one megawatt by adding modular units. “A completed validation program establishes an independently measured performance baseline for larger-scale deployment, permitting, interconnection, and commercialization,” Vivify Technology stated in a press release.According to the company, independent data could help evaluate the technology before wider deployment. Additionally, completing the validation program could support future permitting, grid interconnection, commercialization and wider use. Herring told H2 Tech that the company aims to offer an alternative to traditional energy systems rather than compete within them. “Data centers, disaster zones, military operations, remote industrial sites, even the next frontier beyond Earth – they all point to the same truth: the world needs power that can move, scale, and operate outside the old rules,” he concluded.

title: New sensors aim to bring real-time tracking to nuclear recycling
content: SHINE and GE Vernova are developing a system that could track nuclear material in real time as spent nuclear fuel moves through a recycling facility, with the goal of making the process cheaper and easier to manage.The project, led by GE Vernova’s Advanced Research Center and funded through the US Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), is focused on improving how nuclear material is measured and accounted for during recycling.SHINE, working as a subcontractor to GE Vernova, is developing improved sensor deployment and material-tracking systems. The technology is designed to build material control and accountability directly into a recycling plant rather than adding those systems after the facility is designed.The approach is part of a project called Monochromatic Assays Yielding Enhanced Reliability, or MAYER. It is intended to continuously measure nuclear material as it moves through different stages of a recycling facility and send that information into a virtual digital twin of the process.Real-time tracking cuts costly checksNuclear facilities currently rely on a combination of instruments, physical security measures, manual sampling and periodic shutdowns to determine how much nuclear material is present and where it is located. Those procedures can add significant cost and interrupt operations.MAYER is intended to reduce the need for some of those repeated checks by providing a continuous picture of material moving through the facility. The system could also help operators identify changes in material quantities without having to rely as heavily on manual measurements.“There’s a better way to handle material control and accountability at spent nuclear fuel recycling facilities — one that doesn’t mean permanent cost and disruption,” said Ross Radel, SHINE CTO. “As a company designing a recycling process of its own, SHINE is joining the GE Vernova-led collaboration to tackle the design challenge of building modern accountability and safeguards into nuclear recycling facilities from day one. Get that right, and these facilities will be more cost-effective and have less downtime.”The tracking technology is also tied to nuclear safeguards. Operators must account for nuclear material to ensure it is not stolen or diverted, making accurate inventory measurements a central part of security at recycling facilities.Lowering the recycling burdenFor SHINE, the work has a larger commercial goal. The company is developing its own nuclear fuel recycling process, called Recover Elements – Destroy Undesirables – Create Energy, or REDUCE. The process is intended to recover uranium, plutonium and other valuable materials from spent nuclear fuel.SHINE says improved material tracking and accountability could help its future recycling facilities qualify for a lower-security category under US Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules. That could reduce the amount of physical security infrastructure required and lower operating costs.The company is targeting a commercial pilot for nuclear fuel recycling as the US looks to address the roughly 94,000 metric tons of spent nuclear fuel that has accumulated across the country.The MAYER project is therefore tackling a less visible part of nuclear recycling: knowing exactly where the material is and how much of it is moving through the plant. If the system works as intended, that capability could help make large-scale fuel recycling more practical and economically viable.

title: Taiwan partners with U.S. on 200 nm range submarine drone tech for maritime defense
content: Taiwan is partnering with U.S. defense startup Vatn Systems to develop autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), adding another layer to the island’s growing focus on unmanned systems for maritime surveillance and defense. The agreement was signed between Vatn and Taiwan’s government-funded National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST). Under the memorandum of understanding, the two sides will explore AI-enabled command-and-control systems, autonomous underwater vehicles, and a local supply chain and maintenance network for the technology. The partnership is intended to combine Vatn’s undersea autonomy technology with Taiwan’s research and industrial capabilities, according to NCSIST. Vatn CEO and co-founder Nelson Mills said the company aims to develop affordable autonomous underwater systems for the U.S. and its allies and deploy them at scale. AUVs for a wider range of missions One of the systems involved in the partnership is Vatn’s Skelmir S12, a relatively low-cost and modular AUV that can be configured with different ranges, sensors and levels of precision depending on the mission. The agreement calls for exploring the fielding of the S12 in Taiwan, according to SCMP . Autonomous underwater vehicles can perform missions without exposing crews to the risks associated with operating manned vessels in contested or difficult underwater environments. Their applications can range from seabed mapping and infrastructure inspection to maritime surveillance and mine countermeasures. For Taiwan, the technology also offers a way to expand its underwater capabilities without relying exclusively on large and expensive platforms. The Defence Post reported that Vatn is also developing other undersea technologies, including SIGURD, an autonomous mine-countermeasure system, and a lower-cost inertial navigation system designed for underwater and surface operations where GPS is unavailable. Building Taiwan’s underwater drone capabilities The Vatn agreement is part of a broader effort by NCSIST to develop Taiwan’s autonomous underwater capabilities while working with foreign technology companies. NCSIST is also cooperating with U.S. defense technology company Anduril Industries and is acquiring its Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle. The system can reportedly operate at depths of up to 6,000 meters (19,685 feet) and remain underwater for around 10 days at low speed. According to SCMP, NCSIST officials expect experience with Dive-LD to help develop expertise in autonomous navigation, sensor integration, modular payloads and lower-cost production. At the same time, Taiwan is pursuing indigenous underwater technology through its Huilong program. That effort has produced a 30-meter-long, 100-ton prototype intended to establish technologies that can be developed further through cooperation with U.S. companies. NCSIST has described the approach as a two-track strategy. Leveraging foreign systems and expertise while developing critical technologies, including underwater sensors, domestically. Why underwater drones matter Taiwan’s interest extends beyond military operations. AUVs can inspect undersea cables and other critical infrastructure, map the seabed and support offshore industries. The same basic capabilities can also support military missions such as reconnaissance , mine hunting and underwater surveillance. That dual-use nature is one reason unmanned underwater systems are becoming increasingly attractive. Instead of building a single highly specialized platform, modular AUVs can potentially carry different sensors and payloads for different missions. The Vatn partnership therefore goes beyond acquiring another underwater drone. It gives Taiwan a pathway to work on autonomy, command and control, local sustainment and production while expanding the number of unmanned systems available for operations beneath the surface. For an island whose security depends heavily on its surrounding waters, that underwater capability could become an increasingly important part of its maritime defense architecture.

title: Thorium fuel surpasses 60 GWd/MTU in major test ahead of reactor demo
content: Clean Core Thorium Energy has selected Kinectrics to independently review its ANEEL nuclear fuel qualification program, bringing the thorium-based fuel one step closer to a demonstration in an existing CANDU reactor.The review will examine the fuel’s design, manufacturing process, safety case and regulatory readiness. It is intended to give utilities and other nuclear stakeholders an independent assessment before the fuel moves toward commercial demonstration irradiation.ANEEL combines thorium with enriched uranium and is designed to work with existing water-cooled reactors. The approach could improve fuel utilization while reducing long-lived spent fuel volumes and strengthening safety and proliferation-resistance characteristics.The latest review adds another layer of technical validation to a program that is already moving through testing and manufacturing. BWXT Canada is working on the CANDU fuel bundle hardware, while Canadian Nuclear Laboratories is fabricating full-scale, reactor-ready ANEEL fuel bundles.Thorium fuel faces testingThe fuel has already undergone accelerated irradiation testing at Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Test Reactor, reaching burnups above 60 GWd/MTU. That testing is important because fuel must demonstrate that it can withstand the demanding conditions inside a reactor over extended periods.CCTE has also completed engineering work examining ANEEL’s performance, safety characteristics and compatibility with different reactor designs. The fuel platform is intended for potential use in pressurized heavy water reactors, Generation IV reactors and light water reactors.The company says its design could allow thorium-based fuel to be introduced into existing CANDU reactors without major reactor modifications. That makes the technology different from approaches that require an entirely new reactor system before the fuel can be deployed.“Kinectrics brings world-class expertise in nuclear safety analysis and licensing support, making them one of the most trusted independent evaluators in the nuclear industry,” said Milan Shah, COO of Clean Core Thorium Energy. “With BWXT Canada supplying the fuel bundles and CNL advancing ANEEL fuel pellet fabrication, their independent evaluation provides critical validation as we progress toward regulatory approval and future deployment.”Existing reactors get new fuelThe technical pathway now brings together fuel fabrication, reactor hardware, irradiation testing and independent review. If those stages are successfully completed, ANEEL could provide a route for testing thorium-based fuel in established nuclear infrastructure rather than waiting for new reactor designs to reach commercial operation.The fuel uses thorium alongside enriched uranium, including low-enriched uranium and high-assay low-enriched uranium variants. Its design aims to extract more useful energy from nuclear fuel while potentially reducing the amount of long-lived waste produced for a given amount of electricity.The independent assessment is therefore less about creating a new fuel concept and more about determining whether ANEEL can meet the engineering, safety and regulatory requirements needed for real reactor use.The latest milestone builds on irradiation results and manufacturing work that CCTE says establish the foundation for a commercial reactor demonstration.The engineering assessment was published in the journal Nuclear Engineering and Design.

title: US Air Force-backed KRONOS nuclear reactor gets high-power fuel boost
content: US-based NANO Nuclear Energy and Quadrant Nuclear Industries have signed an initial agreement to secure specialized nuclear fuel. Under this arrangement, the companies will develop plans for the future supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium, known as HALEU. The fuel will come from Quadrant’s planned Vanguard facility at Idaho National Laboratory. This site aims to produce up to eighteen metric tons of enriched fuel each year with support from the United States Department of Energy.The primary user of this fuel will be NANO Nuclear’s KRONOS micro modular reactor. This system is a stationary, high-temperature gas-cooled reactor. Each unit produces between 10 and 45 megawatts of thermal energy. That heat converts to an electrical output of 3.5 to 15 megawatts per unit.Packing more energy into smaller volumeThe choice of fuel is directly tied to the reactor’s compact size. Standard commercial nuclear plants run on uranium enriched up to 5 percent. In contrast, advanced microreactors need uranium enriched up to 20 percent. This higher level of enrichment packs more energy into a smaller volume. It allows the core to operate for much longer periods without refueling. It also lets engineers build far smaller reactor vessels and core structures. However, commercial supplies of this fuel remain scarce. Setting up production and delivery pipelines now is critical for testing, regulatory approvals, and eventual deployment.Notably, conventional reactors mostly rely on large volumes of water to cool their cores. However, the KRONOS system replaces water with inert helium gas, which remains in a single gas phase throughout the cooling cycle without boiling. Because the system requires no external water source, it can run in dry, remote environments where traditional power plants cannot operate.Continuous electricity without grid connectionThe reactor also operates independently from regional power grids. This technical setup led to an earlier Phase I development contract with the United States Air Force through its AFWERX innovation initiative. Military planners are evaluating the design as a standalone power source for remote bases. The system can provide continuous baseline electricity without connecting to civilian grids or depending on regular fossil fuel deliveries.Over the coming years, both companies will work to align their technical systems. Reactor cores require strict tolerances for fuel shape, cladding materials, heat transfer rates, and neutron behavior. The partnership will address these engineering needs alongside shipping logistics, demand projections, and regulatory oversight.“Access to reliable, domestically produced HALEU will be a key element in supporting the growth of advanced nuclear energy,” said James Walker, CEO of NANO Nuclear Energy.By linking fuel manufacturing directly to reactor development, the project aims to solve the technical and supply hurdles facing modern microreactors.“The companies intend to collaborate on areas including fuel supply planning, technical interface requirements, commercial structuring, regulatory coordination, logistics considerations, and demand forecasting associated with future HALEU supply arrangements,” concluded the company in a press release.

title: US fusion reactor firm scales flat superconducting magnets with funding
content: Thea Energy has completed an extension of its Series B financing round to support the engineering and manufacturing of its nuclear fusion systems. The expanded round adds backing from Brevan Howard Macro Venture, Aloniq, ALJ Investments, Beyond Earth Ventures, and other global institutional participants. These funds build upon a previous 100 million dollar investment round led by the US Innovative Technology Fund. The capital is designated to establish a second operating facility in Northern New Jersey, scale domestic magnet manufacturing lines, and accelerate development of the company’s demonstration hardware.Nuclear fusion aims to generate clean, baseload electricity by heating light atomic nuclei into a plasma until they fuse and release energy. Because plasma operates at extreme temperatures, power plant designs must keep it contained inside a vacuum vessel using strong magnetic fields. In the arena of nuclear fusion, magnetic confinement systems have relied on two primary configurations; they are tokamaks and stellarators.Tokamaks generate magnetic fields by driving strong electric currents directly through the plasma itself. While tokamaks are widely studied, these internal currents can cause sudden plasma turbulence and operational disruptions. Solving problems with stellaratorsStellarators solve this problem by generating all necessary magnetic fields from external coils surrounding the vessel. This external approach maintains plasma stability without internal currents. This, in turn, allows the system to operate continuously in a steady state.However, manufacturing standard stellarators is full of hurdles. Conventional designs rely on large, non-planar magnetic coils with complex, twisted geometries.To solve this manufacturing bottleneck, Thea Energy—a spinout from Princeton University—has redesigned the stellarator using flat, high-temperature superconducting magnets. Instead of forcing physical metal coils into complex shapes, the company arranges modular arrays of flat coils around the reactor. Software algorithms then dynamically adjust the electrical inputs to shape the magnetic field computationally. This modular planar architecture allows the hardware components to be built using standard, high-volume production techniques.The company has spent two years developing and validating this magnet architecture. Recent testing confirmed that the planar shaping coils consistently reach the required magnetic strength and spatial precision targets. The company’s first integrated system, named Eos, will incorporate approximately 300 of these planar superconducting coils to sustain steady-state fusion conditions. Engineering teams are currently evaluating prospective sites for the Eos facility.Modeling plasma behaviorTo model plasma behavior prior to physical construction, Thea Energy launched a joint initiative with NVIDIA, Synopsys, Argonne National Laboratory, and the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory. The group is building a digital twin to simulate field interactions and plasma dynamics in real time.These development stages support Helios, the company’s planned commercial power plant design. The preconceptual architecture for Helios was certified by the US Department of Energy through its Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program. In parallel, the company secured a 20 million dollar award from the Department of Energy’s ARPA-E SCALEUP program to expand domestic manufacturing for its modular coils. Alongside these technical milestones, the company is conducting early talks with utilities, hyperscalers, and energy buyers.

title: US seeks to replace aging artillery guns with Korean K9 Howitzer
content: The U.S. Army has selected Hanwha Defense USA’s K9 Mobile Howitzer (K9MH) to build prototypes for its new Mobile Tactical Cannon (MTC) program, marking the South Korean defense company’s first major U.S. Army contract.Hanwha will initially deliver six prototype systems, with an option for another 12. As per reports, the agreement could be worth up to $262.9 million. The prototypes will allow the Army to evaluate the wheeled 155mm artillery system before deciding on potential follow-on production.The award is significant because the MTC program is intended to provide the Army with a more mobile alternative to its M777 155mm towed howitzers. The Army’s prototype solicitation calls for a mature, wheeled 155mm system that can undergo testing and experimentation as a potential replacement for the M777 in some formations.A wheeled version of the K9The K9MH is based on Hanwha’s established K9 self-propelled howitzer family, but uses a wheeled Tatra Force 8×8 chassis rather than the tracked configuration of the standard K9.Hanwha says more than 2,500 K9 systems have been fielded globally, giving the company an existing production and operational base as it enters the U.S. competition. Several U.S. allies, including Australia, Poland and Norway have adopted the K9 family.The MTC requirement is centered on a 155mm cannon, with the Army’s solicitation specifying systems in the 49- to 56-caliber range. The Army is also working on ammunition and propulsion technologies intended to extend the range of future MTC systems.That combination of firepower and mobility is central to the program. A wheeled self-propelled howitzer can relocate under its own power rather than requiring a separate vehicle to tow the gun, potentially reducing the time and personnel required to move artillery between firing positions.Hanwha is also building in the U.S.The Army’s selection is not simply about importing an existing Korean artillery system. Hanwha Defense USA has been developing a U.S. industrial footprint around the K9MH. In April, the company announced that it had leased a facility in Opelika, Alabama, to serve as its initial U.S. integration and testing site for the K9 Mobile Howitzer family. The first phase is expected to create approximately 40 jobs.The company has described localization as a central part of its strategy, with plans to develop domestic production and support capabilities as the program progresses. That industrial component matters because the Army’s MTC solicitation explicitly evaluates more than just the weapon’s technical performance. Prototype proposals were also assessed on U.S. integration, delivery schedule, production cost, supply-chain health and plans for transitioning to domestic production.Six systems first, much larger program possibleThe current award is a prototype contract, not a full-rate production order. The Army will use the initial systems for testing and experimentation before deciding which platform should move forward. The MTC program could ultimately be considerably larger. Industry reporting has put the Army’s broader requirement at roughly 500 systems. At the same time, the Army’s 2027 budget documents allocate more than $1.1 billion across the MTC program’s planned development and production activities over the budget period. For Hanwha, that makes the six-prototype award much more consequential than its initial quantity suggests.The company now has to demonstrate that the K9MH can meet the Army’s requirements in U.S. testing, and that its proposed American production network can deliver the mobility, firepower and industrial capacity the service is seeking from its next-generation Mobile Tactical Cannon.

title: US tests high-speed flywheel for decades-long grid energy storage
content: A US-developed flywheel designed to store electricity without lithium-ion batteries is heading for an independent technical assessment covering its performance, safety, reliability, and commercial readiness.New York-based Qnetic announced on August 18 that its grid-scale Pulsar flywheel system has entered the Electric Power Research Institute’s deRISKED program. Sponsored by the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD), the evaluation will combine prototype data, performance modelling, and pilot-scale testing to help utilities assess the emerging technology using independently reviewed evidence.Flywheel stores electricity mechanicallyUnlike batteries that store energy through chemical reactions, the Pulsar system stores electricity as mechanical energy. It uses a high-speed composite rotor suspended inside a vacuum enclosure.Electricity supplied to the system accelerates the rotor, retaining energy through its rotation. When electricity is required, the stored mechanical energy can be converted back into electrical power.Qnetic says the technology is designed to operate for decades with minimal performance degradation. The company also claims that it can provide virtually unlimited cycling, rapid response times, and predictable lifetime economics compared with conventional battery systems.However, these characteristics will now be examined through EPRI’s established evaluation process rather than being assessed solely through information supplied by the developer.Qnetic is developing Pulsar for several grid-scale applications, including renewable energy integration, grid balancing, microgrids, industrial sites, and energy-intensive data centers.The system is intended to serve markets requiring long-duration energy storage and frequent charging and discharging.Pilot data to undergo independent assessmentQnetic will submit its prototype testing records and a complete set of pilot-system performance data to EPRI. The material will be used alongside standardized testing, technical assessment, and performance modelling.The deRISKED program, whose name stands for Readiness Informed by Shared Knowhow, Evaluation, and Data, was established to assess pre-commercial energy-storage technologies consistently.Its process combines laboratory tests, field demonstrations, and data analysis.“Utilities need objective evidence when evaluating emerging energy storage technologies. Independent validation has become just as important as technical innovation,” said Michael Pratt, CEO of Qnetic. “By participating in EPRI’s deRISKED program and sharing extensive prototype and pilot data, we’re giving utilities the transparency they need to evaluate our technology on its technical merits and better understand where flywheel energy storage delivers the greatest value,” he added.The evaluation is intended to give utilities technical information that can be considered separately from vendor claims when examining possible storage deployments.Findings will be shared with utilitiesEPRI’s program evaluates the performance, functionality, safety, and reliability of emerging storage systems as they move towards commercialization. Its findings are intended to reduce uncertainty for utilities considering technologies that have not yet reached broad commercial deployment.“Independent technology evaluations using consistent analysis methodologies help energy storage stakeholders to objectively contextualize the landscape of pre-commercial energy storage technologies,” said Taylor Kelly, principal technical leader at EPRI. “The deRISKED program supports our participants by sharing information that helps informed decision-making as emerging energy storage technologies move toward commercialization,” he added. The resulting findings will be presented to utilities participating in the deRISKED program.

title: US: Kaleidos nuclear reactor begins 1,000-mile road trip on a truck
content: Radiant’s 1-MWe Kaleidos microreactor began traveling from El Segundo, California, to Idaho National Laboratory on August 12. The reactor is being transported more than 1,000 miles on a trailer bed.At Idaho National Laboratory, Kaleidos will be installed inside the Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments, or DOME, test bed. Radiant will conduct a five-phase testing program covering criticality, heat and power generation, full-power operation and 150 hours of continuous operation without operator assistance.The company will use data from the program for its U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission license application. Radiant is targeting completion of the campaign in the third quarter of 2026.Kaleidos travels from California to IdahoRadiant designed Kaleidos to be transportable by land, sea and air. “We said we’d make a microreactor that is transportable by land, sea and air. We did. Kaleidos is traveling more than 1,000 miles on a trailer bed,” the company said.Radiant said the unit being delivered to DOME uses the same design, scale and commercial fuel load planned for reactors manufactured at its proposed R-50 production facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.“The unit now on its way to Idaho isn’t a simplified stand-in,” Radiant said. “Kaleidos is the same design, at the same scale, with the same commercial fuel load, that will roll off the production line at Radiant’s R-50 factory in Oak Ridge and ship to customers,” they added.Reactor faces five testing phasesDOME uses the repurposed containment structure of a former experimental breeder reactor. The facility allows developers to test experimental reactor designs and collect performance data.Radiant’s five-phase program will begin with zero-power criticality. Testing will then advance to heat and power generation, full-power operation and a final 150-hour continuous run without operator intervention.“Every phase of testing it undergoes, from criticality to 1 MWe thermal operation, to full power, and a capstone 150-hour continuous run without operator intervention, generates data that feeds directly into Radiant’s NRC license application and de-risks manufacturing and deployment at commercial scale,” Radiant said.After Kaleidos is installed inside DOME, it will be loaded with tri-structural isotropic, or TRISO, fuel. The loading will take place under the oversight of the U.S. Department of Energy and Idaho National Laboratory.Standard Nuclear fabricated the fuel to Radiant’s specifications earlier in 2026.First commercial reactor scheduled for 2028Radiant’s Part 70 license application for the proposed R-50 microreactor production facility is under review by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The company is targeting regulatory approval in the final quarter of 2026.The Oak Ridge facility is planned to manufacture commercial Kaleidos reactors for shipment to customers.Radiant has also signed an agreement with the U.S. Air Force to deliver its first commercial microreactor to Buckley Space Force Base. Delivery to the military installation is scheduled for 2028.“Radiant’s testing campaign will ensure we deliver Kaleidos to Buckley Space Force Base by 2028,” the company said.

title: World's most powerful magnetic actuator integrated aboard spacecraft
content: A Los Angeles-based company has achieved a key milestone as its powerful magnetic actuator is flight-ready. Called Supertorquer, the device is expected to become the most powerful magnetic actuator ever flown.Developed by Zenno Astronautics, the Supertorquer is integrated aboard Portal Space Systems’ Starburst-1 spacecraft, which Portal recently revealed publicly for the first time.Next generation of spacecraft capabilities“Portal was built to enable the next generation of spacecraft capabilities, and that means working with partners who are pushing the state of the art,” said Jeff Thornburg, CEO of Portal Space Systems. “Zenno’s Supertorquer is a great example of exactly that. Flying the world’s most powerful magnetic actuator aboard a highly maneuverable spacecraft expands the mission options available to our defense and commercial customers and reinforces what’s possible when advanced technologies are brought together on a single platform.”Supertorquer’s flight heritageThe company also pointed out that the latest reveal marks the next step in the Supertorquer’s flight heritage, following its first launch with Impulse Space.When the November 2025 partnership was announced, the Supertorquer was on track for its first mission with Portal; today it is built, integrated aboard Starburst-1, and moving through the final flight preparations.World-first system that uses superconducting electromagnetics to control a spacecraft’s attitudeThe Supertorquer is a world-first system that uses superconducting electromagnetics to control a spacecraft’s attitude — its orientation— without consuming chemical propellant. The flight unit is designed to generate a magnetic dipole of up to 3,500 A·m², interacting directly with Earth’s magnetic field to provide control authority in MEO and GEO orbits without depleting a consumable resource or competing with the propellant budget reserved for maneuvering, according to a press release. On a mission built around rapid, repeated repositioning, that distinction is the point: every kilogram of fuel Starburst does not spend on pointing is a kilogram available for changing orbits. That powerful magnetic field may also produce another useful effect: radiation shielding, as per the release. Deflecting some charged particles away from the spacecraftThe company also pointed out that by deflecting some charged particles away from the spacecraft, the Supertorquer’s field has the potential to reduce the radiation environment experienced by onboard systems. Zenno’s laboratory testing has shown promising results, and the Supertorquer aboard Starburst-1 will carry a charged-particle counter to measure the effect in orbit.Starburst-1 is Portal’s first free-flying mission with live payloads, designed to demonstrate rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO), rapid retasking, and rapid orbital change for national security and commercial operators. The mission will run for a one-year primary campaign and will also validate subsystems shared with Portal’s larger trans-orbital vehicle, Supernova, including the high-performance RCS thrusters that serve as Starburst’s main translational propulsion.

title: Zhuque 3 Rocket: China lands commercial 217-foot reusable rocket for the first time
content: China’s LandSpace successfully launched the 66-meter (217-foot) Zhuque-3 rocket into orbit and vertically recovered its stainless-steel first stage in Gansu province.It quietly stole a victory right out from under Elon Musk’s nose. This marks the world’s first stainless-steel booster recovery following an orbital launch. SpaceX has been racing to land its massive stainless-steel Super Heavy booster, which is awaiting regulatory approval for its own orbital recovery attempt. LandSpace is now the fourth entity globally to recover a launch vehicle.As per the state news agency Xinhua, the launch happened from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert at 7.35 am on Wednesday, August 19. After delivering a Honghu-3 internet satellite into orbit, the rocket’s first stage returned to Earth. It made a precise vertical landing in Minqin County, Gansu Province — roughly 390 kilometers (242 miles) southeast of its Gobi Desert launch site.MISSION SUCCESS | ZhuQue-3 Y2 Reusable Launch Vehicle Achieved Full Success in Orbital Insertion and First-Stage RecoveryOn August 19, 2026, at 07:35 (UTC+8), the ZhuQue-3 (ZQ-3) Y2 reusable launch vehicle lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Pilot Zone.… pic.twitter.com/fshijOxgtc— LandSpace (@LandSpace_Tech) August 19, 2026Steel in the skyJust eight months ago, the company’s maiden attempt ended in a fiery explosion three kilometers above the desert floor when a descent engine failed to reignite. Engineers spent the intervening months stripping down flight telemetry, rewiring ignition sequences, and prepping a second hull. This time the company made it. The achievement propels LandSpace into an elite global club of companies that have successfully recovered an orbital launch vehicle. These include only four entities: SpaceX, Blue Origin, China’s state-space agency, and now LandSpace.This milestone gives China a crucial edge in its space race with the US. China is locked in a fast-paced race to build its own global satellite internet networks, dubbed Guowang and Qianfan.Designed to compete directly with Starlink, these megaconstellations require placing tens of thousands of satellites into low Earth orbit. But Beijing has faced a major hurdle: a lack of cheap, reusable launch capacity.While Starlink has used reusable Falcon 9 rockets to launch over 10,000 operational satellites, China’s networks have stalled at roughly 200. Without a reusable workhorse, scaling up is economically impossible.Zhuque-3 could help change that. SpaceX dominates the race Zhuque-3 becomes China’s second orbital rocket to achieve first-stage recovery, following the state-owned Long March-10B’s successful offshore net capture in July. Positioned in the same class as SpaceX’s Falcon 9, both Chinese rockets offer similar heavy-lifting capability into low Earth orbit. Zhuque-3 is capable of hauling 18 tonnes to orbit in reusable mode. The rocket provides the exact lifting power Beijing needs to begin mass-deploying its constellation.LandSpace designed the Zhuque-3 with two key technical upgrades over SpaceX’s Falcon 9: a stainless-steel airframe and a liquid methane-oxygen propulsion system. Replacing aluminum-lithium alloy with stainless steel enhances heat resistance while potentially lowering manufacturing expenses. In addition, powering the rocket with methane and liquid oxygen provides a cleaner burn than the Falcon 9’s kerosene-based propellant mixture, which reduces engine soot and streamlines post-flight refurbishment for quicker reuse.Reportedly, the Zhuque-3 booster has been designed to fly up to 20 times over its operational life. For comparison, SpaceX routinely launches its Falcon 9 around 150 times a year and and frequently reuses individual boosters for dozens of missions.SpaceX proved that reusability lowers the cost of reaching space. China has now proven it can play the exact same game using stainless steel and methane fuel. But Musk’s company already has a vast reach with over 12 million active customers worldwide, making it a dominant player in global satellite communications.

title: Gold electrodes account for most of perovskite solar cells' environmental impact
content:
Gold electrodes account for most of perovskite solar cells' environmental impact
Researchers at the University of Palermo and the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology have published a life-cycle assessment (LCA) and cost analysis of four lab-scale perovskite solar cells developed under Italy's NEST (Network 4 Energy Sustainable Transition) project, identifying the environmental and economic bottlenecks that stand between current lab performance and industrial competitiveness.
Solar PV's installed capacity has grown roughly tenfold over the past decade, and perovskite solar cells are widely seen as one of the more promising next-generation technologies to sustain that growth. But as the technology moves toward commercialization, the researchers argue that its environmental footprint and manufacturing costs need to be designed in from the early research stage rather than addressed after the fact - an approach known as eco-design. To that end, the team applied the Product Environmental Footprint methodology and life-cycle costing to four cells fabricated in NEST partner laboratories in Rome and Palermo, quantifying impacts and costs per kWh of electricity generated over each cell's lifetime.
The analysis identified the gold electrode as the dominant environmental hotspot by a wide margin, accounting for more than 90% of the impact in categories including acidification, freshwater ecotoxicity, eutrophication, human toxicity, land use, and mineral and metal resource use, along with 75-79% of global warming potential. A sensitivity analysis showed that cutting gold consumption to best-available-technique levels - roughly a hundredfold reduction - would cut mineral and metal resource use by around 94 times, several other impact categories by 60 to 90 times, and global warming potential by roughly 3.6 times. The authors point to carbon-based, graphene, or dielectric-metal-dielectric electrode structures as viable substitutes, which could also enable semi-transparent applications such as building-integrated PV windows and greenhouse agrivoltaics.
The study also found that today's lab-scale cells carry a considerably heavier environmental footprint per kWh than commercial silicon modules - roughly 1.4 times higher global warming potential, 1.5 times higher fossil resource use, and triple the mineral and metal resource use - largely because low efficiency and short operating lifetimes reduce the total electricity generated over a cell's life. Scenario modeling showed that reaching 25% power conversion efficiency with a 15-year operating lifetime would be enough to bring the cells' lifetime energy output, and therefore their per-kWh footprint, roughly in line with commercial silicon.
On costs, fabricating the lab-scale cells ran €6.02 to €10.09 per cm², with materials, dominated by the gold electrode, accounting for 99% of that figure. Converted to a levelized cost of electricity, that works out to €7.6–17.9 per kWh, one to two orders of magnitude above current commercial solar PV. The researchers note that the same gold-reduction measures identified in the environmental analysis would also cut fabrication costs by roughly a third. They point to established alternative manufacturing routes, including roll-to-roll, blade coating, and slot-die coating processes, to replace lab-scale spin coating - alongside electrode material substitution as the practical path toward industrial-scale, cost-competitive production.

title: Chinese automotive glass giant announces vehicle-integrated solar roof - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Fuyao Glass has confirmed mass-production capabilities for solar sunroof glass, with photovoltaic cells embedded in laminated automotive glass to power auxiliary vehicle loads. While reports have linked the technology to BYD models and cited high output and efficiency figures, these claims remain unconfirmed as Fuyao advances commercialization of vehicle-integrated PV.
Vincent Shaw
19 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
The world’s largest automotive glass manufacturer, Fuyao Group, has confirmed that it has developed solar sunroof glass incorporating photovoltaic cells and has the capability to manufacture the product at scale, following earlier reports linking the technology to BYD vehicles.
Fuyao said the product embeds solar cells within laminated automotive glass, allowing sunlight to be converted into electricity for auxiliary vehicle loads. The company describes the technology as a “solar sunroof,” rather than a photovoltaic system covering the entire vehicle roof. According to Fuyao’s official product information, the electricity can be used to power onboard electrical equipment.
The technology is not entirely new to Fuyao. In May 2024, the company told investors that it had achieved mass-production capability for solar sunroof glass and was supplying the product for vehicle programs where customers required it. The latest disclosures therefore appear to signal progress toward commercialization rather than the completion of the technology itself.
Several Chinese automotive media reports since February have claimed that the system was jointly developed with BYD and would be offered on the Han and Tang models for an optional price of CNY 8,000 ($1,190). Other widely circulated figures include a peak output of 720 W and a conversion efficiency of 23.18%, based on heterojunction (HJT) solar cell technology.
However, neither Fuyao nor BYD has published technical specifications or a joint announcement confirming those figures. During a March investor briefing, Fuyao declined to identify its customers or disclose pricing, saying both were commercially confidential.
Fuyao recently said its factories in Fuqing Yangxia and Hefei had each reached production capacity of 3 million sets of automotive glass by the end of 2025 and were ramping up production in 2026. It has not disclosed what proportion, if any, of that capacity is dedicated to solar sunroofs.
Vehicle-integrated PV (VIPV) is unlikely to replace conventional EV charging because of the limited surface area available on passenger cars. Its more immediate role is likely to be supplying low-power auxiliary loads while vehicles are parked, potentially reducing battery drain and supporting ventilation and other standby functions. Fuyao’s move toward volume production suggests that automotive PV is shifting from a largely experimental application toward a more commercial product.

title: Czechia’s largest BESS goes online - pv magazine Global
content: From ESS News Czech industrial holding Suas Group and Slovak investment firm EIF have energized a 57 MW / 120 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in near the town of Lipnice nad Sázavou, located in Czechia’s Vysočina Region, some 100 kilometers southeast of Prague. The 400 million CZK (USD 19.1 million) Lipnice BESS is now the largest operational battery storage system in Czechia. The second-largest is the 37.95 MW/41.7 MWh BESS at the Modlany Energy Park in northern Czechia , which was commissioned earlier this month. The two companies said the facility can be used to help maintain the stability of the Czech electricity system, provide ancillary services to Czech transmission system operator ČEPS, or participate in commercial arbitrage on the day-ahead and intraday electricity markets. The facility comprises 144 battery cabinets, 18 power conversion systems, and nine transformer skids. “The storage facility could supply electricity to a city the size of nearby Sokolov for ten hours,” the joint statement reads. “It is a key tool for optimizing electricity trading and managing imbalances effectively.” “It makes no sense to base the battery economy solely on providing technical flexibility,” the two companies went on to say. “Therefore, we will use BESS Lipnice primarily on the daily and intraday market.” Suas Group believes BESS Lipnice will pay for itself within five to eight years, supported by revenues from multiple electricity markets and smart algorithmic management. The future of the Czech Republic’s energy storage market will be driven by utility-scale investments and favorable regulations, according to analysis by Aurora Energy Research from November 2025. The agency forecasted the country’s total battery storage capacity to hit 6 GWh by the end of the decade. In March 2025, the European Union approved an aid package for 1.5 GWh of storage capacity in the Czech Republic. The post Czechia’s largest BESS goes online appeared first on pv magazine Global .
