title: Researchers Discover a Mysterious New Frog Species in the Amazon
content:
In addition to expanding scientific knowledge about Neotropical amphibians, identifying new species has a direct impact on conservation strategies. Credit: CBioClima
A small frog living in a flooded corner of the Amazon has turned out to be something scientists had never formally recognized before.
Some species hide in remote places. Others hide in plain sight.
In the western Brazilian Amazon, scientists have identified a new frog species, Adenomera varcena, living in forests that are seasonally submerged by rising rivers. The tiny amphibian looks so much like its close relatives that appearance alone was not enough to distinguish it. Its identity emerged only after researchers combined DNA evidence with mating-call recordings, physical measurements, museum comparisons, and details about its habitat.
That detective work revealed more than a new name. The frog appears to occupy an environment that is unusual for its relatives, offering another example of how much biological diversity can remain hidden even within groups that scientists have studied for years.
Amazon Floodplain Frog Discovery
Researchers encountered
A. varcena
during expeditions in the Upper Juruá River region of Acre, near the Moa and Crôa rivers and the city of Cruzeiro do Sul. Its name refers to várzea forests, the Amazonian floodplains that are periodically inundated as rivers rise.
Other closely related Adenomera frogs are generally associated with terra firme forests, areas that remain above seasonal floodwaters. The new species therefore expands scientists’ understanding of the ecological range occupied by the genus.
Flooding is not simply a temporary disturbance in várzea forests. It is one of the forces that defines these ecosystems, repeatedly changing which parts of the forest floor are accessible to terrestrial animals. For a small frog whose reproduction depends on local environmental conditions, that makes its choice of habitat particularly important.
Hidden Species and Cryptic Diversity
The discovery illustrates one of the persistent challenges of cataloging tropical biodiversity: different species can look remarkably similar.
Scientists call this cryptic diversity. Animals that appear nearly indistinguishable may belong to separate evolutionary lineages, meaning traditional visual identification can miss species that have been hiding in collections or field records for years.
That is effectively what happened here.
A. varcena
belongs to the
Adenomera simonstuarti
species complex, a group in western Amazonia that genetic research had already shown contains multiple distinct lineages. Several of those lineages still lack formal scientific descriptions.
DNA and Frog Calls Reveal a New Species
To establish
A. varcena
as a separate species, researchers brought together DNA data, recordings of its calls, body characteristics (morphology), habitat information, and comparisons with preserved museum specimens.
One subtle physical clue is the absence of a dark marking on the underside of the forearm. Its mating call provides another identifying signature. The frog produces a short call with an unusually slow rhythm and distinctive acoustic properties compared with related species.
For frogs, sound can be especially revealing because mating calls help individuals recognize suitable partners. Differences that seem minor to human ears can therefore help expose evolutionary boundaries that are almost invisible from appearance alone.
The Amazon may contain many more frogs like this
Undiscovered Frog Diversity in the Amazon
The finding adds to growing evidence that the number of Amazonian species visible on paper does not necessarily reflect the diversity actually living in the forest.
Within the
A. simonstuarti
complex alone, earlier genetic work identified numerous distinct lineages across western Amazonia. The newly named frog resolves the identity of one of them, while others remain undescribed.
A biological population cannot be properly evaluated as a distinct species for conservation purposes until scientists know what it is, where it occurs, and how it differs from its relatives.
Climate Change Threatens Specialized Habitat
The problem becomes more urgent when a species is tied to a specialized habitat.
“Since we don’t yet know in detail the species’ ecological requirements and its natural history [reproductive period and mode], it’s difficult to predict the impacts of climate change, which may alter the seasonal flooding patterns of the floodplain forest ecosystem in this region of the Amazon,” says Thiago R. Carvalho, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG).
“Since the species has a preference for this specific ecosystem, it’s possible to suggest that these changes in flood dynamics may influence—though we don’t know to what extent—the species’ reproductive behavior. In a scenario of accelerated loss of natural areas, the formal description of a new species underscores how much more effort we still need to make to advance studies on our biodiversity. Species may become locally extinct even before they’re formally recognized as species through their naming and description.”
Naming Species Can Help Protect Them
Célio F. B. Haddad, a professor at São Paulo State University (UNESP), argues that the pace of habitat loss makes taxonomic work increasingly consequential.
“Currently, the pace of ecosystem destruction outpaces the capacity of taxonomic studies to keep up. Consequently, species that haven’t yet been described are omitted from lists of threatened fauna and remain legally and environmentally vulnerable. Thus, describing new species serves as a tool that aids in their protection. Furthermore, deepening our knowledge of actual biodiversity expands our understanding of the evolution of organisms, consolidating an essential pillar for both pure science and conservation strategies,” he says.
Formal recognition does not automatically protect an animal. It does, however, give conservationists and government agencies a defined species that can be mapped, studied, and considered in extinction risk assessments and environmental decisions. Furthermore, without a scientific name and a clear description, an uncommon species can effectively disappear inside data assigned to a more widespread relative.
Reference: “A New Species of Terrestrial Foam-Nesting Frog (Adenomera, Leptodactylidae) from the Várzea Forests of Western Amazonia” by Marianna S. Borburema, Leandro J. C. L. Moraes, Marcus Thadeu T. Santos, Santiago R. Ron, Célio F. B. Haddad, Ariovaldo A. Giaretta and Thiago R. Carvalho, 15 May 2026,
Ichthyology & Herpetology.
DOI: 10.1643/h2025033

title: Scientists Discover a Surprising Link Between Human Genes and Language
content:
Some of the world’s most genetically isolated populations are also home to unusually diverse language structures. The pattern hints that long-term separation may preserve forms of linguistic variation that sustained contact tends to erase. Credit: Shutterstock
Human migration and isolation appear to shape genetic and language diversity in opposite ways.
The finding may seem counterintuitive at first. Regions shaped by migration and population mixing often have higher genetic diversity, so it might seem logical that their languages would be more varied too. Instead, the study finds the reverse pattern.
“We were struck by how robust this inverse relationship is across the globe,” says Anna Graff, lead author of the study and linguist at the
University of Zurich
. “Places where people have mixed more tend to be genetically diverse, but their languages are structurally more similar. In contrast, places with long-term isolation show less genetic diversity, yet much greater diversity in how languages are structured. Crucially, this relationship holds after adjusting for a wide range of confounding factors, including deep population history such as the timing of continental settlement.”
Linking genes and language
To identify the pattern, the study combined large-scale genetic and linguistic datasets. The analysis compared genetic variation among individuals with structural variation among languages in each region.
It also accounted for other possible influences, including geographic closeness, population density, and environmental conditions, making it possible to better isolate the role of demographic history.
Contact, migration, and isolation are formative forces
The analysis revealed a strong global pattern: contact, migration, and isolation shape both human genetic diversity and language structure, but they do so in opposite directions.
“The key insight is that contact and isolation have opposite effects on genes and languages,” explains Chiara Barbieri, senior author and population geneticist at the University of Cagliari. “Contact increases genetic diversity, but it also promotes the spread of linguistic features, making languages more similar. Isolation, by contrast, limits genetic diversity while allowing languages to evolve independently.”
Languages and human DNA both capture aspects of human diversity. Credit: UZH, NCCR Evolving Language
Genetically isolated regions are hotspots of linguistic diversity
This pattern helps explain why certain parts of the world are especially rich in linguistic diversity. New Guinea and the Himalayas, for example, are relatively genetically isolated, yet their languages show exceptional structural variety.
“Such hotspots give us a glimpse of what languages can do when evolving under conditions of relative isolation,” says Balthasar Bickel, senior author and Director of the Institute for the Interdisciplinary Study of Language Evolution at the University of Zurich. “They preserve a wider range of ways of organizing grammar, sound and meaning, a range that cannot be observed elsewhere because it got reduced by long histories of contact.”
Beyond revealing a striking worldwide pattern, the study points to a larger lesson: language diversity is closely tied to the history of human populations. “What might initially look like a paradox turns out to be a simple and actually intuitive principle,” Graff concludes. “The same processes that keep populations apart allow languages to grow apart as well.”

title: Scientists Find Just 3 Minutes of Sprinting Can Transform Blood Chemistry
content:
Exercise intensity may shape the body’s chemical response as much as exercise duration. Many proteins that reacted strongly to sprinting were also linked in large population data to lower risks of metabolic and cardiovascular disease. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
A few minutes of sprinting triggered a much larger immediate molecular response than prolonged moderate exercise and altered proteins linked to better metabolic health.
Just three minutes of intense sprinting can produce molecular changes in the bloodstream that look very different from those seen after much longer periods of moderate exercise.
Researchers at
Rockefeller
compared several exercise intensities and found that six 30-second, all-out sprints changed nearly one quarter of the proteins they measured immediately after exercise. By comparison, 90 minutes of continuous moderate cycling affected fewer than one quarter of one percent. Moderate treadmill running altered more proteins than cycling, but still far fewer than sprinting.
Sprinting rapidly reshapes blood chemistry
The effects extended well beyond proteins. Sprinting changed more than 200 metabolites and produced an immediate rise in proteins involved in blood vessel growth, tissue remodeling, and hormonal signaling.
Some appeared to reach the bloodstream through ectodomain shedding, a rapid signaling process in which portions of proteins already positioned on cell surfaces are cut away and released into circulation rather than being newly produced. Human fat cells exposed to blood collected after the sprints also showed widespread shifts in gene activity affecting fuel processing, hormone responses, and nutrient sensing.
Moderate exercise produced a smaller and slower molecular response. A substantial wave of fatty acids and proteins originating from the liver, which commonly appear as the body responds to the demands of endurance exercise, did not emerge in the blood until three hours later. Human fat cells exposed to blood taken after moderate cycling showed only modest changes in gene activity.
Sprint-responsive proteins track better health
The researchers next compared proteins affected by exercise with health information from more than 53,000 participants in the UK Biobank. Many of those proteins were associated with lower risks of cardiovascular and metabolic disease. The pattern was especially strong for obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic disorders. Of 33 proteins associated with lower risk, sprinting altered 32, while moderate exercise changed only three. More than one quarter of the proteins were also associated with slower biological aging.
“What’s exciting here is that just a few minutes of intense exercise can trigger a significant molecular response,” says Paul Cohen. “And we still see it after eight weeks of training, which tells us this response isn’t simply a product of the body struggling to keep up with unfamiliar stress. It may be that the responses we observed are intrinsic to intense exercise.”
“It’s well appreciated that different intensities of exercise stimulate distinct body-wide adaptations,” notes Luke Olsen, the postdoctoral fellow who conducted the studies. “However, the molecular mechanisms linking these intensity-dependent adaptations have remained largely elusive. Our work suggests that exerkines–proteins and metabolites released into the bloodstream following exercise–are highly sensitive to exercise intensity and may be the key mediators of the health-promoting effects of short bursts of vigorous exercise.”
Reference: “Exercise intensity modulates interorgan communication and is associated with cardiometabolic health outcomes in humans” by Luke Olsen, Javier Botella, Douglas Barrows, Ethan Romero, Kaitlyn Baird, Mutsumi Katayama, Ece Kilic, Christopher Peralta, Nadège Zanou, Henry Sanford, Laurie Farrell, Christopher L. title: Scientists Find a Surprising Diabetes-Fighting Compound in Turmeric
content:
A compound in turmeric may do more than curb inflammation: in rats with Type 1 diabetes, curcumin appeared to protect blood vessels from changes linked to cardiovascular disease. Credit: Shutterstock
Curcumin improved blood vessel health in diabetic rats, but human benefits still need to be tested.
For people with Type 1 diabetes, controlling blood sugar is only part of the challenge. Over time, persistently elevated glucose can damage blood vessels, helping drive a higher risk of cardiovascular disease even when insulin therapy is carefully managed.
Now, researchers are exploring whether a familiar compound from turmeric could help counter some of that damage. Curcumin, the pigment that gives turmeric its vivid yellow color, is known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. In a new rat study, it also appeared to preserve the structure and function of the aorta and improve several cellular processes disrupted by diabetes.
“Curcumin acts as more than a simple compound found in a spice or an antioxidant. It not only helps to improve blood sugar levels but also reduces inflammation, restores cellular responses, and preserves both structure and function of the aorta in Type 1 diabetes,” said the study’s first author, Swasti Rastogi, a PhD candidate at Florida Institute of Technology.
The findings, presented in Minneapolis at the 2026 American Physiology Summit, suggest curcumin may influence multiple pathways involved in diabetes-related vascular injury. About 2 million people in the U.S. live with Type 1 diabetes, a lifelong autoimmune disease in which the body cannot produce enough insulin, making cardiovascular complications an important long-term concern.
Curcumin improved vascular health
To investigate curcumin’s potential effects, researchers studied rats with Type 1 diabetes and compared animals that received curcumin with diabetic rats that did not. After one month, the curcumin-treated rats had healthier blood vessels that more closely resembled those of rats without diabetes.
The treatment appeared to lower inflammation, restore normal calcium activity in blood vessels, and rebalance heat shock protein 70, an important protein that diabetes can disrupt. Taken together, these changes suggest that curcumin may help limit the damage diabetes causes to blood vessel structure and function, including the gradual loss of strength and elasticity that can raise the risk of heart disease.
Human use remains untested
Turning these results into a treatment for people with Type 1 diabetes would take much more research than simply recommending extra turmeric or curcumin supplements. Because the work was done in rats, clinical studies are still needed to determine whether curcumin can safely benefit people, what dose might be effective, and how it could interact with medications they already take.

title: Scientists Reveal How ADHD Could Fuel Creative Thinking
content:
ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, impulse control, and activity levels. While it can make everyday tasks more challenging, research is also exploring how ADHD-related attention patterns may contribute to creativity, flexible thinking, and intense focus in certain situations. Credit: Shutterstock
ADHD-related attention patterns may become a source of creativity and focus when supported through structured creative expression.
How can ADHD create serious everyday challenges for millions of people while also appearing among highly successful creative figures such as Justin Timberlake and Simone Biles?
New research from Constructor University neuroscientist Dr. Radwa Khalil, published in
iScience
, examines the neuroscience behind that apparent contradiction by looking at how creativity and attention are connected in the brain.
The study shows that some mental processes linked to ADHD, including defocused attention, can also support creative thinking when they are guided in useful ways. Its findings point to possible creative therapies using art, music, and dance as effective nonpharmacological options for the nearly 8% of children worldwide affected by ADHD.
Attention may widen creativity
The study, written with researchers from several leading French research institutions, points to a changing view of ADHD.
“There’s a tendency to view attention-related conditions like ADHD purely through the lens of deficit: what is wrong, what is missing, or what needs to be fixed?” said Dr. Khalil. She noted that although ADHD is often understood as a deficit, emerging evidence shows that attention and creativity rely on shared neural networks.
“Neurodivergent attention patterns, then, are not merely problems. They can open pathways to powerful creative thinking when directed appropriately,” she said.
The study brings together findings from multiple fields to show that creativity and attention processing involve overlapping brain networks. It also describes how free associative thinking, which can generate creative ideas, is connected with distractibility, mind wandering, and other behaviors often seen in ADHD.
Dr. Radwa Khalil, Neuroscientist with Constructor University. Credit: die Zeit
Dr. Khalil used an analogy to make the connection easier to understand: “Think of attention like a spotlight. Most people are able to focus their beam on one thing. ADHD brains have a wider spotlight, taking in more information at once. This condition can make routine tasks that require focus challenging. However, this broader view, or ‘defocused attention,’ also encourages exploratory thinking and new idea combinations, which fuel creativity.”
The healing power of creativity
Dr. Khalil and her colleagues see meaningful therapeutic potential for people with ADHD and related conditions. Creative practices such as art, music, dance, writing, gaming, and other activities can give individuals with ADHD structured ways to direct and explore their defocused attention. These activities may also help strengthen brain networks involved in attention control, potentially reshaping patterns tied to impulsivity and hyperactivity.
“Authentic creative expression is so much more than a pleasant distraction,” continued Dr. Khalil. “It is engaging the same neural circuits involved in attention control, essentially providing a workout for the brain. For a child with ADHD, the experience of getting ‘lost in the moment’ when creating art or playing music may actually be strengthening their ability to focus by working with their natural cognitive style instead of against it.”
Although the findings are encouraging, Dr. Khalil and her colleagues stress that the relationship between attention and creativity is still not fully understood. To move the field forward, the study lays out a framework for future research, emphasizing collaboration across disciplines, new methods, and long-term studies. Dr. Khalil argues that any major change in ADHD treatment must begin with a broad research agenda that brings together neuroscientists, art therapists, clinicians, and other specialists.
Reference: “Attention unleashed: Creative therapy for thoughtful transformation” by Sarah Bou Sader Nehme, Emiliano Macaluso and Radwa Khalil, 15 May 2026,

title: Scientists Spotted This Mysterious Congo Monkey 18 Years Ago – Now They Finally Know What It Is
content:
Colobus congensis, known locally as “likweli,” has a dramatic black face with pinkish-orange lips. Credit: Junior Amboko, Florida Atlantic University
A newly identified Congo monkey represents an ancient evolutionary lineage that may already be endangered.
A partly hidden monkey appeared in a photograph taken deep in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in 2008. Researchers saw the animal again a decade later, this time clearly enough to begin investigating whether it represented something science had never formally described.
Genetic, anatomical, and acoustic evidence has now confirmed that the elusive primate is a distinct species. Named
Colobus congoensis
and called “Likweli” by local communities, it is only the fifth new monkey species identified in Africa within the past 75 years, making the discovery an unusually rare event in modern primatology.
The animal lives in a remote section of the Congo Basin between the Lomami and Congo (Lualaba) rivers in east-central DRC. Despite decades of biological research across Central Africa, this isolated population had remained undocumented.
The first obscured image in 2008 provided little more than a clue. A clearer photograph obtained in 2018 prompted a broader search involving field observations, local knowledge, museum specimens, and laboratory analyses.
Junior Amboko (left) and Mardoché B. Koko working in the field in the Lomami National Park. Credit: Junior Amboko, Florida Atlantic University
The results, published in
PLOS One
, show that
C. congoensis
belongs to an evolutionary lineage that separated from its closest known relative roughly 4 to 5 million years ago. They also indicate that the newly recognized species may already face serious pressure from hunting, habitat loss and an exceptionally restricted range.
The international investigation included researchers from Florida Atlantic University, the Lukuru Wildlife Research Foundation, Yale University, the City University of New York, Lomami National Park and the Frankfurt Zoological Society.
“This discovery is both exciting and deeply personal, highlighting the extraordinary biodiversity of my homeland and how much remains undocumented,” said Junior Amboko, co-corresponding author, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biological Sciences in FAU’s Charles E. Schmidt College of Science and a National Geographic Explorer. “I was honored to name the species ‘
Colobus congoensis
,’ recognizing the Congo Basin’s remarkable natural heritage and, we believe, marking the first primate named after the Democratic Republic of Congo itself – underscoring both its global importance and local pride.”
Colobus congoensis map. Credit: John Hart, Lukuru Wildlife Research Foundation
A monkey unlike any known colobus
C. congoensis
weighs about 15 pounds, making it smaller than related colobus monkeys. Its glossy black coat forms cape-shaped shoulders and extends into a long tail, while an orange cream patch surrounds its mouth and nose.
Long black facial hairs, large folded ears and reflective fur create a distinctive mask-like appearance. White markings around the animal’s rear provide another feature separating it from other known members of the group.
The discovery further establishes Lomami National Park and its surrounding buffer zone as an important center of primate diversity. Several members of the same research collaboration helped identify another previously unknown monkey from the region in 2012, the Lesula (Cercopithecus lomamiensis).
“We continue to be reminded that the Congo Basin remains one of the world’s last great frontiers for mammal discovery,” said John A. Hart, first author and a conservation scientist with the Lukuru Wildlife Research Foundation. “Even in regions that have been scientifically explored, entirely new species are still coming to light. This discovery reinforces how much biodiversity remains undocumented in the Central Congo Basin and how this region continues to reshape our understanding of primate evolution and conservation.”
DNA reveals a four million year split
DNA evidence placed
C. congoensis
within the genus Colobus, but its closest evolutionary connection was unexpectedly distant in both geography and time.
“The discovery of
Colobus congoensis
is reshaping our understanding of African monkey evolution,” said Kate Detwiler, Ph.D., senior and corresponding author and an associate professor of biological sciences in FAU’s Charles E. Schmidt College of Science. “Its closest known relative is Colobus satanas, found more than 1,200 kilometers away in west-central Africa. Yet our genetic evidence shows the two species diverged roughly 4 to 5 million years ago, marking one of the oldest known evolutionary splits within the Colobus lineage.”
Colobus congoensis and C. satanas in life. (A & B) C. congoensis, Lomami National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo. Credit: (A) Daniel Rosengren, (B) Bravo Bofenda. (C & D) C. satanas, Lope National Park, Gabon. Photo credits: (C) Martin Royele/Royele Safaris, (D) Barna Takats.
Researchers also needed physical evidence to establish the animal as a formally recognized species. They compared its skull, teeth, face and pelt with those of other African colobine monkeys, looking for a combination of features that could not be explained as ordinary variation within an existing species.
“We compared the skulls and pelts of
C. congoensis
with other species of African colobines, which underscored how unique this new species is,” said Julia L. Arenson, Ph.D., co-author and a postdoctoral associate at the Yale Institute for Biospheric Studies, who had a very large collection of skeletal data related to her Ph.D. thesis on colobus monkeys. “At the same time, despite being much smaller in body size, we also demonstrated it shares features of the teeth, skull and face with Colobus to the exclusion of other African colobines.”
Colobus congoensis, known locally as “likweli,” has deep resonant roaring calls that resemble those of related Colobus species but possesses a distinct acoustic structure. Credit: Bernard Bonanga
These cranial and dental comparisons supported the DNA results and supplied the anatomical diagnosis required to validate
C. congoensis
scientifically.
“In order to name a new species, you have to be able to prove it,” said Christopher Gilbert, Ph.D., co-author and an anthropology professor with the City University of New York Graduate Center and Hunter College. “We used extensive museum collections including specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and the American Museum of Natural History, and comparative datasets to compare the skulls and pelts with known African colobus monkeys. This robust pool of information allowed us to pretty quickly and conclusively confirm
C. congoensis
as a new species.”
Its calls provided another line of evidence. Although the monkey produces the deep roaring vocalizations typical of related Colobus species, recordings revealed an acoustic structure distinct from those of its relatives.
A photograph of Colobus congoensis, whose common name is the local vernacular name, “likweli.” Credit: Daniel Rosengren
Local knowledge reveals a tiny range
To determine where the monkey lives and how often it is encountered, researchers spoke with hunters and other residents in villages surrounding Lomami National Park. Only people in eight villages recognized the animal or described it accurately.
Residents called it “Likweli” and “kasaba nkoni,” which means “the branch shaker.” Their accounts consistently portrayed it as an elusive monkey that is rarely observed.
Fieldwork from 2018 through 2022 produced 114 sightings within an estimated area of only 1,700 square kilometers. That is an unusually restricted distribution for a colobus monkey.
The species appears confined by major rivers, forest barriers, and its reliance on scattered patches of upland forest. These natural boundaries may help explain how the population remained separated long enough to follow its own evolutionary path.
Discovery comes with an extinction warning
Formal recognition has also exposed how vulnerable
C. congoensis
may be. Its known population occupies a very small region already affected by forest loss and increasing hunting pressure.
Researchers are proposing that the species be listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List because of its restricted range, apparently small population, and continuing threats to its habitat. Most confirmed locations fall within Lomami National Park, making continued protection of the park and its forests especially important.
“The discovery of
Colobus congoensis
is both a scientific triumph and a sobering reminder that some of Earth’s rarest creatures may vanish before the world even knows they exist,” said Detwiler.
Reference: “Likweli: A remarkable new species of Colobus monkey from the Lomami National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo” by John A. Hart, Junior D. Amboko, Julia L. Arenson, Emma R. Horton, Kathryn F. Coates, Jean-Pierre I. Kapale, Mardoché B. Koko, Terese B. Hart, Christopher C. Gilbert, Eric J. Sargis and Kate M. Detwiler, 15 July 2026,
PLOS ONE
DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0349857

title: Why Does an Irregular Heartbeat Strike 40 Years Early in Some People?
content:
Atrial fibrillation, or AFib, is a common heart rhythm disorder in which the heart’s upper chambers beat rapidly and irregularly instead of contracting in a coordinated way. Credit: Shutterstock
A hidden genetic threat may trigger atrial fibrillation decades early, raising the risk of stroke before symptoms appear.
Atrial fibrillation (AFib) occurs when chaotic electrical signals cause the heart’s upper chambers to beat irregularly and out of sync with the lower chambers. Blood can then collect inside the heart, creating clots that may travel to the brain.
Recent estimates suggest that at least 10.55 million American adults, roughly one in 22, have AFib, making it far more common than previously believed. Although the condition is strongly associated with aging, high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease, inherited risk can bring it on much earlier.
“For many people, their first symptom of AFib is a stroke,” said Dawood Darbar, the new chair of the Department of Medicine at Penn State College of Medicine, who has spent his career investigating abnormal heart rhythms. “If we can prevent even one stroke, the impact on that person and their family would be huge.”
When Genetic Risks Combine to Disrupt the Heart
Darbar led a multi-institutional study published in
Nature Communications
that investigated why a rare mutation does not affect everyone who inherits it in the same way. The researchers found that its effects can be intensified by numerous common DNA differences, each of which contributes only a small amount of risk on its own. In an analysis of the U.K. Biobank, people carrying a heavy burden of these common risk variants had about twice the likelihood of developing early-onset AFib.
The team examined a rare mutation in LMNA, a gene that helps organize DNA inside cells. The mutation changed how tightly parts of the genome were packaged, making it harder for cells to access and activate genes that help regulate the heart’s electrical rhythm. Common genetic variants further weakened this control, showing how rare and widespread forms of genetic risk can combine to produce disease much earlier in life.
In this Q&A, Darbar explains how heart cells generate a coordinated beat, why inherited mutations alone do not tell the entire story, and how combining different forms of genetic risk could eventually help doctors identify vulnerable patients before AFib leads to a stroke.
Q. What happens when the heart beats? What breaks down during AFib?
Every heartbeat begins with an electrical impulse generated by specialized cells in the heart’s natural pacemaker. This impulse travels through the upper heart chamber, or atria, causing the heart muscle cells to contract in a coordinated fashion and pump blood into the bottom heart chambers, known as ventricles. The electrical signal then passes through the ventricles, producing the heartbeat that pumps blood throughout the body.
In AFib, this orderly electrical system breaks down. Instead of a single, coordinated electrical impulse, multiple abnormal signals spread through the atria simultaneously. As a result, the atria “quiver” rather than contract effectively, leading to an irregular heartbeat and increasing the risk of stroke, heart failure, and other cardiovascular complications.
Q: AFib is usually described as a disease of aging. Where do genetics come in?
Most AFib is related to high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease. But roughly 20% is genetic. Some people inherit a rare genetic mutation that substantially increases their risk of developing AFib at an early age. However, in our recent study in Nature Communications, we saw that these mutations do not act in isolation.
Each of us also carries hundreds or even thousands of common genetic variants — or single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), pronounced “snips” — that individually have only a very small effect on AFib risk. But when many of these common variants occur together, they can amplify the impact of a rare AFib-causing mutation. It’s the interaction between rare and common genetic variants that appears to matter.
We refer to this as “additive” risk because rare and common genetic variants work together to provide a more complete picture of a person’s likelihood of developing AFib than either type of variant alone. In our analysis of the U.K. Biobank, a health and genetic database that includes more than 500,000 participants, individuals with a high burden of common genetic risk variants had approximately twice the risk of developing early-onset AFib.
Q. What is an example of this additive effect?
Some families carry a rare mutation in a gene called LMNA, which helps organize DNA inside the cell. LMNA mutations have been linked to inherited forms of heart disease and AFib. In our study, the mutation altered how tightly certain regions of DNA were packaged, which in turn affected how easily those regions could be accessed and regulated.
Using blood samples—donated by individuals with and without AFib—to generate personalized human heart cell models, we found that the rare LMNA mutation and SNPs converged on many of the same DNA regulatory pathways. Several of those SNPs were located within regions of DNA whose accessibility had been altered by the LMNA mutation. One of these regions helps regulate the movement of sodium ions into heart cells, a process that is essential for generating and conducting the electrical signals that produce a normal heartbeat.
This provides a concrete example of additive genetic risk: the rare LMNA mutation creates a vulnerable cellular environment, while a person’s background of common genetic variants can further increase or modify that risk. Together, these factors may help explain why some people develop AFib much earlier than others. It also suggests that predicting AFib risk may require looking beyond a single harmful mutation and considering a patient’s broader genetic landscape
Q: What does this all mean for a patient sitting in your clinic?
These studies were conducted in laboratory-based cell models, so the findings are not yet ready to guide routine clinical care. What they do provide is a clearer understanding of how rare and common genetic risk factors can converge to disrupt the heart’s electrical system. With additional research, including studies in patients, this knowledge could eventually help us identify who is at greatest risk for developing AFib at a young age.
Genetic testing is already an important part of evaluating patients with inherited heart rhythm disorders and their families because it can identify people who may be at increased risk before symptoms appear. In the future, combining information about a rare disease-associated mutation with a person’s broader genetic background may allow us to estimate risk more accurately, for example, identifying someone who may be more likely to develop AFib in their 30s or 40s.
Our findings also suggest that LMNA should be considered in genetic testing panels for inherited arrhythmia syndromes. LMNA has traditionally been associated with cardiomyopathy and heart failure, but our work shows that some individuals with LMNA variants may first present with AFib, before structural heart disease becomes apparent. Identifying these patients earlier could lead to closer monitoring, earlier treatment, and screening of family members who may also be at risk.
The long-term goal is to move from reacting to complications to preventing them. For example, if we can identify a high-risk individual early, we might use a wearable heart monitor to detect AFib before it causes a stroke. That would be a very different and much more proactive conversation than the one we are often able to have with patients today.

title: Anthropic’s Enterprise AI Venture Buys Consultancy
content: A joint venture established by Anthropic and Wall Street firms such as Blackstone has made its first acquisition since its July launch as it looks to boost the growth of Claude, Anthropic’s chatbot, among businesses. Anthropic ’s venture, called Ode with Anthropic, plans to announce Thursday that it is buying an AI consultancy, Casper Studios, which helps businesses develop applications using AI, according to Ode. It’s making the acquisition at a time when corporate executives are trying to figure out how to get the most from AI and are wary of rising bills from the new technology. “You can actually accomplish a lot of what you need…using all of the tooling that Anthropic is building on top of their models,” said Chris Taylor, CEO and co-founder of Ode. The four-year-old Casper Studios employs a dozen or so technical consultants. Casper says it has worked with Netflix, Pepsi, private equity firms and hedge funds. The purchase price couldn’t be learned. Headquartered in San Francisco, Ode currently employs over 100 people, who often work alongside Anthropic engineers to integrate AI into businesses in industries such as accounting and healthcare. It launched in July after the Anthropic–private equity joint venture bought Fractional AI, another applied AI services firm that Taylor and Ode Chief Technology Officer Eddie Siegel founded together. Earlier this summer, Ode announced it would be building custom products with IT consulting firms Baker Tilly and Citrin Cooperman. Anthropic is in the midst of unprecedented growth, largely based on the strength of its AI coding models, which appeal to developers even as costs per user have jumped . Businesses such as retailer Restoration Hardware are also buying Anthropic’s Claude chatbot and related tools, enabling their workforces to automate finance, project management and other tasks. Anthropic is trying to beat back a charge from OpenAI, which is reorienting itself as an enterprise-focused firm, and from open-source models that could help buyers save on costs. But Anthropic and OpenAI have each acknowledged that for some businesses, using AI isn’t a cinch—hence the need for consultants, also known as forward-deployed engineers. These consultants often work on-site with customers to help them organize their files and proprietary data so the AI can make sense of it, and also to help them develop apps for automating functions such as customer support. OpenAI is a major investor in its own joint venture to sell AI to enterprises, The Deployment Co., which has raised $4 billion at a $10 billion valuation from backers including TPG, Brookfield Asset Management, Bain Capital and Advent International. The Deployment Co. has used some of its new money to buy firms that employ hundreds of the consultants helping companies integrate customized AI models and systems. Meanwhile, Thrive Holdings, a one-year-old holding company started by OpenAI investor Thrive Capital, recently raised $2 billion from outside investors. It takes stakes in and operates companies that own small accounting and services businesses: The idea is to transform those traditional businesses by automating routine work. OpenAI provides researchers as well as product and engineering for the venture, though Thrive Holdings’ businesses aren’t restricted from using non-OpenAI models, including open-source ones. Anthropic created Ode with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs, Sequoia Capital and other firms, which together invested $1.5 billion in the new company. Many of the companies Ode does work for  are backed by the private equity firms.

title: Enovix Next-Gen Batteries Are Terrific. Are They Also Obsolete?
content: In August 2022, Ananda Baruah, a technology analyst with Loop Capital, doubled his price target for next-generation battery developer Enovix to $100 a share. At the time the stock was trading around $20. Other leading analysts were less bullish, but Baruah argued that the startup was on the cusp of a windfall in sales to some of the biggest names in technology and cars. Four years later, those sales have yet to materialize, as the company has had trouble scaling up its expensive battery and others have caught up to it technologically. This week, investors lost patience. After the company on Monday announced the resignation of CEO Raj Talluri, who said he had taken another job, Enovix’s stock price fell 18% to $3.14. On Monday evening, Executive Chair T.J. Rodgers held a call with analysts to try to quell the investor revolt. He said the company was on track for big sales of batteries for smartphones, smart glasses and drones. It didn’t help. On Tuesday, Enovix’s share price fell another 13%, a total two-day drop of 29%, though it recovered by 10% in midday trading today. On top of that, the company’s thrashing appeared to spread to battery rivals: Amprius Technologies shares fell 7% on Tuesday, QuantumScape 6% and SES AI 7%. Baruah has cut his target price to $15 a share, conceding that the company’s revenue prospects, at least for the time being, are a lot less than what he had expected. On Monday, investment bank William Blair downgraded the stock, and Bank of America and Cantor Fitzgerald lowered their price targets for the company. This week’s walloping of next-generation battery stocks reflects the genuine risk these startups face. While most of them have recently begun to earn their first commercial revenue , delivering batteries to the booming drone and AI data center industries, the number of next-gen startups seeking this business is high. That suggests that at least some of them will be left with just crumbs. And these startups cannot rely on future business from electric vehicle makers, which so far have snubbed next-gen batteries in favor of cheap conventional ones, whose performance has steadily improved in recent years. But Enovix could have a harder time than most of its rivals. It’s not that its battery is technically flawed: According to disclosed metrics, the company makes a terrific product with energy density of a whopping 935 watt-hours per liter, meaning its batteries could power smart devices using AI features for hours, and roughly 50% longer than conventional lithium-ion batteries with graphite anodes. In his call with analysts, Rodgers also said Enovix could now deliver 1,000 charge cycles, considered a minimum in many electronic devices. But the company’s battery is exceptionally costly, and it has had a hard time speeding up production and decreasing its manufacturing defect rate at its plant in Malaysia. Danny McInnes, a private investor in Scotland who tweets about Enovix frequently on X, bought shares in the company when it went public in 2021, but, worried about its manufacturing difficulties, he sold the stock a year ago. “I think we end up coming back to the nagging question of ‘Can they make this battery at high yields?’ I have seen no concrete evidence that they can,” McInnes told me in an exchange of texts. In 2021, I attended a party at Enovix’s headquarters in Fremont, Calif., held to celebrate its listing on the Nasdaq Stock Market. Enovix’s secret sauce was that it had developed a tiny stainless steel cage that could safely contain a silicon battery anode, a prized material because silicon can theoretically hold 10 times as much lithium as conventional graphite anodes. A battery containing a silicon anode would last a lot longer. Enovix’s cage was critically useful because silicon swells and contracts dangerously during the charge-discharge cycle, eventually creating large cracks in the battery. Because the silicon was in a cage that contained the swelling, the Enovix battery would not crack. At the party, co-founder Harrold Rust told me that eager customers were already lining up to order the company’s batteries, which he assured me would appear in a commercially sold smart watch within a year. Over the subsequent months, analysts told me those customers included large names like Meta Platforms. Five years later, Enovix is still waiting to get its battery into a smart watch or any other commercially sold product, though Rodgers said in this week’s call that the company is in the midst of shipping 50,000 sample cells to a smart glasses customer. He didn’t name the customer, but said it planned to install the batteries in test devices “to make sure our stuff works exactly right in their environment.” What’s happened in those intervening years is that batteries as a whole have substantially evolved, arguably eclipsing Enovix’s original advantage. U.S.-based Sila Nanotechnologies has commercialized silicon-carbon anodes in batteries powering combat drones, and Group14 Technologies, another U.S. rival, has deployed its silicon-carbon anodes in batteries for Chinese smartphones. Both of the companies say their anodes contain the swelling. While the Sila and Group14 batteries are also expensive, Enovix’s batteries are even more so. This is partly because it costs a lot to make the unusual stainless steel cage, and also because Enovix doesn’t make the silicon-carbon anodes that go into the cage but buys them from an outside party, so its customers in effect pay for both technologies. That raises the question of why a customer wouldn’t just buy a Group14 anode deployed in a cheaper conventional battery, excluding the cage. The question is at the heart of why Enovix’s future may be limited even if it can successfully scale up its manufacturing. Is there something materially better that Enovix’s battery can do that a cheaper one cannot? Enovix has an answer. In a statement, the company said its rivals had not delivered a battery whose anode contains more than 32% silicon, while the samples that Enovix is currently shipping boast 100% silicon content. (Both Group14 and Sila say their material can be used in a 100% silicon carbon anode.) Whether customers are convinced, though, is the more important issue.

title: Nvidia Discusses Funding Its AI Data Supplier Mercor at a $20 Billion Valuation
content: Nvidia has discussed an investment in Mercor, a data labeling provider that helps the chip designer develop its open-source AI models, according to a person with knowledge of the process. The investment would be part of a $20 billion-valuation round. Existing investor General Catalyst has been in talks to lead the round. Historically, most of Mercor’s revenue has come from the makers of closed-source AI models such as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic, The Information previously reported . But Mercor’s revenue from Nvidia is growing as the chip firm prioritizes the development of its Nemotron open-source models, which aim to compete with the world’s best open models. Last quarter, Nvidia paid Mercor tens of millions of dollars, according to the person and another with knowledge of the contracts. Nvidia also uses data from other providers including Turing and Scale, in addition to its in-house data team, according to those people. (Nvidia invested in Scale’s 2024 funding round that valued the startup at $14 billion. Meta Platforms last year took a 49% stake in Scale and hired its CEO.) Mercor and the other data labeling firms hire human experts in different fields to use and evaluate AI models in specialized tasks. The process generates data that the model makers use to refine the models to improve their capabilities in such tasks, which range from scientific research to legal and finance projects and, according to a Mercor job posting, even programming Nvidia’s graphics processing units. Nvidia used Mercor data in its two latest Nemotron models, according to the company’s disclosures. Reflecting the tightening relationship between the firms, a handful of Mercor employees are focused almost entirely on their company’s work with Nvidia, said the two people. Despite rising spending on such human-generated data, an executive said that Nvidia, like many other AI model developers, relies heavily on synthetic, or AI-generated, data to train its Nemotron models. Nvidia also receives critically useful data when developers access Nemotron models through OpenRouter, a service that helps developers use models from multiple providers, according to another person who worked on Nemotron. The size of Nvidia’s proposed investment in Mercor and the total funding round couldn’t be learned. Mercor generated $614 million in gross revenue in the first half of the year, up 70% from all of last year, The Information previously reported. It paid about 60% to 70% of its gross revenue to contractors as of last year, implying its net revenue in the first half of this year could be roughly between $180 million and $250 million. It expects gross revenue to total $2 billion this year. It swung to a small operating profit last year and has told investors it expects the measure to rise to $226 million this year and $1.7 billion next year. In recent months, Nvidia has been ramping up the pace and scale of its investing, though it primarily pumps money into its direct customers, such as upstart cloud providers, or the biggest users of its chips, such as OpenAI. In the quarter ending in April, it poured $18.6 billion into private companies and infrastructure funds, more than it invested in all of 2025. This year alone, Nvidia has written separate $2 billion checks into cloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius, which buy Nvidia chips, as well as Lumentum and Coherent, which make lasers for Nvidia’s networking hardware. It has also funded a smattering of smaller startups that rent or buy Nvidia chips. The three-year-old Mercor has raised about $520 million from investors including Benchmark and Felicis, according to PitchBook, and was valued at $10 billion in October.

title: Robots Are in Their GPT-2 Era
content: It’s no secret that AI-powered robots aren’t so good yet. They struggle with a broad range of simple tasks, from untangling cables to chopping vegetables. Nonetheless, morale is high among roboticists who are flush with venture cash as they work toward a “ ChatGPT moment ” when robots become broadly useful and available. Until then roboticists are happy to celebrate little milestones. I spent two days this week at Actuate , a robotics conference in San Francisco, along with 1,200 founders, developers and engineers, where I saw demonstrations and video footage showing signs of progress. When Chelsea Finn , a Stanford University professor of computer science and electrical engineering, played a clip of a mechanical robot arm successfully making a latte, the audience broke into applause—no matter that it moved slowly and a human had to steam the milk. (Some robot baristas are already serving coffee, for example at the SFO airport, but software code controls their actions, rather than a single AI model like PI’s that is trained to perform a variety of tasks.) Finn, who is also a co-founder of robotics software firm Physical Intelligence , said her field resembles language AI in the era following OpenAI’s release of GPT-2 in 2019, when large language models were beginning to perform a variety of tasks without being specially trained or fine-tuned to specific ones. PI’s latest model similarly works out of the box on some limited tasks, such as using a pair of robot arms with pinchers to fold laundry and cardboard boxes. The companies I talked to at the event were eager to tinker with AI models for robots and accommodate their limitations. Foxglove , the data startup that hosted the conference, announced new software that lets customers use text prompts to search through troves of video and other physical AI data collected from sensors on their robots, drawing on one of Nvidia’s Cosmos world models to understand which video clips are most similar. That’s a relatively humble use of Cosmos, given Nvidia’s ambitions that world models—AI models designed to produce physically-realistic predictions—will someday power robots directly or generate simulated worlds for robots to learn in. But it stands to make Cosmos genuinely useful right now. Robotics companies are also falling back on humans when AI makes a mistake. Avea Robotics , a startup providing software for remote controlling robots, showed off how an operator in Mexico City could take over a robot when it made a mistake and guide it to successfully plug in an ethernet cable, similar to the way self-driving vehicle companies like Waymo hand over control to remote human operators if they need to. The idea of a “ChatGPT moment” for robotics also calls to mind humanoid robots in particular, whose five-fingered hands could allow them to handle a wide variety of work. But the dream for robotics foundation models is that they will power a variety of robots, from robot dogs and drones, all the way to highly specialized machinery. That might feel far off right now, but if anything, the vibes in robotics are even more positive than they were for language models in the GPT-2 era. It’s worth remembering that developers who used GPT-2, three years before ChatGPT, were over the moon about using the model for primitive chatbots and autocompleting lines of code. While scaling up from GPT-2 looked promising, it was not yet known whether language models could grow up into the sophisticated models we have today. Now that language models have blazed the trail, and self-driving cars have extended AI into the physical world, roboticists expect progress in AI that can power a variety of robots to perform a variety of tasks will follow. “We are on an inflection point where we are seeing signs of generalization, and we can see models getting better and better. And very soon we’ll have a ChatGPT moment,” said Jay Chooi , co-founder and CEO of Robocurve , a startup that evaluates the capabilities of physical AI models. Sure, there are questions about the path to that moment, such as what kind of training data and what kind of AI model will make it possible. But roboticists seem confident that progress is assured. One sign of that progress arrived Wednesday, when startup Generalist announced its latest AI model for powering robots. Generalist found that the model could sometimes control a pair of robot arms to complete tasks such as unzipping a purse and pulling out dollar bills after seeing an example of a person or robot doing the same task. A robot model that can learn from a real-world example would be more akin to GPT-3 , which OpenAI released in 2020. To achieve general-purpose robots, “there’s a very long road ahead,” said Generalist CEO Pete Florence , but the ability to pick up new skills from examples in a prompt has been thought of as “the most vivid, important kind of waypoint along the journey.” Whether Generalist’s new model ends up bringing robotics into the GPT-3 era remains to be seen. For now, the model will only be available to a handful of companies that Generalist is working with. Here’s what else is going on… Overheard OpenAI is preparing to roll out a system to analyze user interactions with its models for cybersecurity and other safety concerns without storing customer data, in a move that positions the company to potentially lure customers frustrated over how Anthropic has handled similar issues. OpenAI plans to launch the new system, dubbed Private Safety Processing, next month, executives said on Wednesday. President Donald Trump said U.S. regulators are working to bring Hyperliquid, a popular offshore venue for perpetual futures, to the U.S. The price of Hyperliquid token jumped 22% after the remark.If Hyperliquid enters the U.S., it will bring a competitor to Coinbase and Kalshi, which recently got approval to offer perpetual futures, which are contracts that allow traders to bet on the price of crypto or other assets with leverage without an expiry date. People on the Move Tim Luke , a vice chairman in Barclays global technology investment banking group, is joining Morgan Stanley as a senior investment banker, according to people familiar with his move. Big Number Shares of Chinese humanoid robot maker Unitree Robotics soared on the debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange on Wednesday, after raising 6.1 billion yuan ($905 million) in an initial public offering. The shares surged more than seven times its IPO price before closing 460% up, valuing the company at slightly more than $60 billion, underscoring Chinese investors’ euphoria in humanoids. 27.3% of the companies dissolved by SimpleClosure , a startup that helps businesses shut down and sell off their assets, were in the SaaS sector from January to June 2026, compared to just 14.4% in AI. Companies that shut down typically recover between $10,000 and $100,000 by liquidating assets to tech buyers, research labs, and AI companies. Stripe announced Wednesday that it agreed to acquire OpenRouter , a marketplace that aggregates AI models, seeking to position itself at the center of payments to AI firms. Stripe is paying $7.5 billion for OpenRouter, of which $1.5 billion is paid to the startup’s founders and $6 billion to investors, the New York Times reported. ALSO , a company that offers small electric vehicles — consumer electric bikes and commercial delivery quads — and is now extending them to drive themselves, raised $150 million in a Series D funding round led by Prysm Capital . title: Stripe Takes OpenRouter
content: No one would ever call payment processing a glamorous business, although if anyone could make it interesting, it’s Stripe’s founders, the Collison brothers (they’re Irish, and one of them has a podcast set in a pub!). Stripe has been out of the limelight for a while, but that’s changed in recent weeks based on speculation that it has been involved simultaneously in a bid for PayPal and talks to buy OpenRouter. On Wednesday, Stripe confirmed one of those deals : the purchase of OpenRouter, which is like a retail store that sells access to hundreds of AI models, including the leading ones from Anthropic. Essentially, OpenRouter makes it possible for businesses and consumers to pick and choose different AI models through a single provider and billing system. Stripe may have another deal coming soon: A report last Friday in The Wall Street Journal suggested the PayPal acquisition was also getting closer. We’ll see how that shakes out over time. But the OpenRouter purchase is arguably more forward looking. (For more on Stripe’s business trajectory and its sudden interest in M&A, see this story .) OpenRouter is an increasingly valuable business, thanks to the growing need businesses have for AI technology. Indeed, OpenRouter’s monthly revenue has more than tripled to about $13 million since April, we reported Tuesday . Despite that spectacular growth, the price Stripe is said to be paying looks a little over the top. Stripe didn’t disclose it, but reports on Monday and today suggested it was around $7 billion to $7.5 billion. That’s quite the appreciation on OpenRouter’s valuation of $1.3 billion from May, when it last raised money . Sure, its business is exploding—but competition is also increasing. As we reported , several companies are contemplating entering the sector, and rivals such as Vercel are already in it. OpenRouter has an early lead, but it’s unclear how much of a moat it has. And given how quickly this market is changing, who can be confident OpenRouter’s position is unassailable? If this deal turns out to be an overpriced bust, the good news for Stripe is that as a private company, it can easily keep the embarrassing details under wraps. Incidentally, it’s a pity Stripe's founders can’t keep under wraps their belief that the singularity has started. Let’s hope this OpenRouter deal wasn’t predicated on that wacky concept. (For more on OpenRouter, see here and here .) Unitree’s Pop Now that’s a first-day IPO pop! Shares of Chinese humanoid robot maker Unitree closed up 460% at its public market debut in Shanghai on Wednesday. That puts SpaceX’s opening-day pop of 18.5% into perspective. It’s been a while since the U.S. markets have seen a tech IPO open this strongly. Older folks might recall the 1999 (dot-com era) IPO of VA Linux Systems, which sold computers that ran on the Linux open-source operating system. That IPO was priced at $30 and rose about 700% to close at $239.25 on its first day, according to this Wall Street Journal account . In recent years, the period of late 2020–21 stands out for frothy pops. That’s when DoorDash opened with an 86% pop, Airbnb rose 112% on its first day and Snowflake more than doubled . We all know what happened next. title: The Hot New Prediction Exchange You’ve Never Heard of—by Design
content: A new behind-the-scenes exchange called Rothera is betting it can capture a significant share of prediction market trading without running its own consumer app. Prediction markets are dominated by Kalshi and Polymarket, which operate consumer-facing apps as well as exchanges that also handle trades for outside firms. Rothera is taking a different approach, offering outside financial firms like retail brokerages an exchange to handle prediction contracts without competing for their customers directly. Rothera hopes to win business from brokerages and other firms looking to tap the fast-growing market for trading on sports, elections and other events. It already has a major brokerage partner in Robinhood, which backed Rothera last fall in a joint venture with trading firm Susquehanna International Group. Both began routing some prediction bets through Rothera this summer. Besides Susquehanna, other trading firms are serving as market makers on Rothera, buying and selling contracts to make small profits and keep trading active. But Rothera wants to go broader and is in talks with more retail brokerages that could send their customer orders to the exchange, co-founder and CEO Thomas Chippas said. Chippas previously was founding CEO of ErisX, a spot crypto market that exchange giant Cboe acquired in 2022. He launched Chicago-based Rothera last year, along with another ErisX alum, Matt Trudeau, as Kalshi and Polymarket were surging in popularity. They saw an opening for Rothera to take orders from firms known as futures commission merchants, regulated intermediaries that sit between customers and exchanges. FCMs can include firms like retail brokerages and banks—Robinhood, for example, operates a FCM through its derivatives trading arm. Rothera doesn’t serve individuals directly and has no plans for a consumer app. “There’s a gap in the marketplace,” Chippas said. “We don’t own a market maker. We don’t own an FCM. It removes a lot of friction rather than directly competing with them.” The two raised money from Robinhood and Susquehanna as both were growing fast in prediction markets , with Robinhood customers flocking to the bets and Susquehanna making markets. Both initially predominantly relied on Kalshi to execute the trades. Rothera needed licenses from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates U.S. prediction markets, to launch an exchange. Those approvals can take years. So in November, it made a $79 million deal to buy most of a licensed derivatives exchange and clearinghouse from Miami International Holdings, which scooped up that licensed business, then known as LedgerX, in FTX’s 2023 bankruptcy. That deal closed in January. Robinhood and SIG each have 45% ownership of Rothera while MIAX owns the remainder, and Rothera isn’t seeking additional funding. (Rothera declined to comment on whether founders have equity.) Despite that ownership, Rothera runs as an independent firm with its own board of directors, technology and licenses. The exchange has about 50 employees and is hiring more. Rothera started trading prediction market contracts in June and already ranks among the five largest exchanges by volume. With Robinhood involved, Rothera didn’t “have to worry on day one where the customers will come from,” Chippas said. “They are an enormous engine and distribution.” Rothera executed about a third of Robinhood’s prediction market volume in June and about 28% in July, according to data firm Artemis. Rothera sees room to win business beyond its backers. In traditional markets, exchanges often operate separately from brokerages and banks. Running an exchange is costly and heavily regulated, and it makes little sense for everyone to build their own and spread trading volume too thinly. Retail brokerages offer the most obvious place for Rothera to expand, given that several besides Robinhood already offer prediction contracts or could add them relatively quickly. Other firms, such as banks that offer derivatives to big customers for hedging or speculation, could move more slowly. "The interest we are seeing primarily is coming from retail FCMs in terms of immediacy,” Chippas said. “The institutions are interested and engaged, but they have a few more hoops to jump through.” Many institutional investors are interested in trading on economic outcomes more than sports, which still dominate prediction market activity. And big traders like hedge funds typically trade through banks’ prime brokerages, which provide financing and other services and would need to get on board. There are still some basics to build out. Banks need teams to support trading around the clock, including weekends, since many prediction-related events take place outside market hours. And banks need software tailored to prediction contracts, though there have been recent advances in that area—bank technology providers FIS and ION both recently launched systems enabling brokers to process prediction market trades 24/7. Rothera’s ambitions could reshuffle an already competitive market. Kalshi recently topped $4 billion in annualized revenue and is close to raising fresh funds at a $40 billion valuation. It’s been aggressively signing up investing apps, including Webull, Coinbase and Moomoo, plus platforms for big investors, including Tradeweb and Talos. Kalshi has even asked banks seeking roles in its potential initial public offering to offer its contracts to clients. Investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald announced on Wednesday it is letting its institutional clients hedge and trade on Kalshi’s event contracts. Polymarket, meanwhile, has partnered with Blockchain.com. Still, there’s little chance one exchange will take all. Financial firms often use several exchanges to compare pricing and avoid disruption if one goes down. Interactive Brokers, for instance, enables trades across Kalshi, CME Group and ForecastEx, its own exchange. Even Robinhood has said it plans to keep using multiple venues. title: 中核西仪废物桶贮存井打磨机器人完成现场测试
content:
2026-08-20 09:03 来源：中核西仪
放射性废物贮存井
近日，由中核西仪研制的废物桶贮存井打磨机器人，在徐大堡3、4号机组工艺性BOP(三废)贮存井打磨工程中正式完成现场测试，标志着核工业在深井受限空间自动化建造领域取得实质性突破。
废物桶贮存井井深大、开口小、垂直度要求高、粉尘浓度高，传统人工打磨需多人轮换进入受限空间，施工周期长且风险高。中核西仪开发的打磨机器人搭载XYZ三轴移动机构和R旋转、W调宽的多自由度运动系统，作业覆盖面宽12米，最大打磨深度5米，可适用于核电各堆型标准废物桶贮存井建造过程。该机器人设备采用远程操控模式，操作人员于井外远程操控，机器人可自动完成进给、旋转打磨并联动吸尘装置集中收尘等多项井四壁与底面全区域打磨操作。
▲打磨机器人工作状态
现场实测显示，打磨后内侧面垂直度4毫米、上下部同轴度偏差3.4毫米、侧面及底面平整度小于2毫米，均优于垂直度≤5毫米、同轴度≤5毫米、平整度≤2毫米的验收标准，各项施工指标满足用户单位施工技术要求，单井作业时长由传统人工的1天压缩至1.5小时，效率提升约81%。该成果实现了人员不下井、远程全流程控制，规避了受限空间窒息、碰撞等施工风险，消除粉尘职业危害，系统性提升了项目施工效能。
徐大堡项目作为集团公司首个深井空间自动化打磨应用案例，为集团同类项目推广应用提供重要参考与成功借鉴。后续，中核西仪将深化工程机器人在核设施建造关键工序的落地，为核电工程智能建造提供装备支撑。

title: 徐大堡核电厂1、2号机组全范围模拟机正式投用
content:
2026-08-20 08:37 来源：中核辽宁核电有限公司
8月19日，徐大堡核电厂1、2号机组全范围模拟机投用仪式在模拟机主控室举行。辽宁核电党委书记、董事长陈劲，总经理、党委副书记张雄出席仪式，中核武汉党委书记、董事长高顺龙应邀出席。仪式由辽宁核电副总经理李祝三主持。
仪式现场，与会人员共同观看模拟机建设历程回顾视频，双方领导共同为“CAP模拟机训练中心”揭牌。
高顺龙表示，模拟机投用是项目建设的重要里程碑，也是全新的工作起点。中核武汉将全力做好模拟机运维保障与优化升级，以此为契机，与辽宁核电拓展合作广度与深度，携手助推项目高质量建设。
陈劲代表辽宁核电党委向模拟机项目全体参建者致以衷心感谢，并对下一步工作提出三点要求：一是严守核安全底线，高标准严要求开展模拟机培训工作;二是持续深化双方合作，确保模拟机长期稳定运行;三是锚定工程建设目标，砥砺奋进，全力推动项目高质量建设。
辽宁核电、中核武汉相关领导及项目负责人参加仪式。下一步，辽宁核电将正式启动1、2号机组首批操纵人员模拟机培训，为后续机组调试和运行夯实人才根基、筑牢核安全屏障。

title: 新加坡代表团到访生态环境部核与辐射安全中心开展交流
content:
2026-08-20 13:42 来源：生态环境部核与辐射安全中心
8月17日，新加坡国立大学核研究与安全所首席执行官刘昕炜、新加坡国家环境局代理局长苏文迪一行到访生态环境部核与辐射安全中心(以下简称中心)，开展核安全领域交流活动。中心副主任李斌及相关部门人员参加活动。
李斌对新方的到来表示欢迎，并向新方系统介绍了中国核能发展现状、核安全监管历程以及核安全监管与技术支持机构的组织架构与职能定位。他重点阐述道，作为国家核安全局直属的唯一从事核安全与辐射环境监督管理技术保障的技术支持机构，中心全面承担核安全审评、辐射环境监测、事故应急、科技研发及国际合作等核心任务，是国家核安全技术审评中心、技术研发中心、信息交流中心和人才培养基地。针对新方关切，中心还详细介绍了在核安全审评中的校核计算与试验验证工作情况。
新方对中心在核安全监管审评方面的丰富经验及过硬的技术支持能力给予高度评价。苏文迪女士表示，2025年她曾作为国际专家参与国际原子能机构(IAEA)对中国的核与辐射安全监管综合评估(IRRS)，对中心的软硬件设施与技术能力印象深刻。此次再度到访，她进一步见证了中心在核安全科技创新、智慧监管及风险防控等领域取得的显著成效。
双方一致认为，中新两国在生态环境与核安全领域具有良好的合作基础。自2023年12月两国签署环境合作谅解备忘录并将核安全与辐射防护列为重点合作领域以来，双方的互信与合作不断深化。新方希望以此次交流为契机，重点在以下五个方面加强与中心的对话与合作：一是小型模块堆审评经验交流;二是适应性监管方法探讨;三是技术支持机构能力建设;四是科研能力建设与人员培训;五是专家互访与交流。
访问期间，李斌还陪同新方实地参观了核与辐射应急大厅、热工水力实验室及核安全软件共享中心等设施。

title: 核电运行研究院落棒时间集成测量技术实现国际授权突破
content:
2026-08-20 15:22 来源：核电运行研究院
近日，核电运行研究院“一种与棒位测量设备集成的控制棒落棒时间测量方法”正式获得美国专利商标局授权，成为公司首个获得海外授权的发明专利。
控制棒落棒时间是保障核电站安全运行的关键参数，通常需在切断棒位探测器激磁电源的情况下进行测量，大修期间测量需反复进行信号接线拆装，占用关键路径时间;功率运行期间意外落棒情况无法追溯分析。
本专利技术由核电运行研究院牵头，与多个电厂专家一起协同完成。将落棒时间测量功能与全数字化棒位测量技术一体化集成，实现了棒位探测器带电运行情况下棒位测量设备自动感知落棒动作并完成数据记录与分析，有效解决了上述工程难题。
目前，该专利技术已在国内核电厂四台机组实现落地应用，适用于300MW、600MW及其他M310系列机组，具有较大的应用市场与社会经济效益。
此次海外专利的获批，是核电运行研究院紧密围绕现场需求自主创新、与电厂协同创新的典型案例，为拓展潜在海外市场创造了有利条件。

title: 生态环境部华北核与辐射安全监督站筑牢田湾核电防汛防台安全防线
content:
生态环境部华北核与辐射安全监督站筑牢田湾核电防汛防台安全防线
当前，正处迎峰度夏和防汛保电重叠的关键时期，江苏省连云港市先后遭遇台风“白海豚”“巴威”影响，强风、暴雨、高温交替来袭，核电站安全运行面临多重考验。为精准防范极端天气引发的设备故障、厂区内涝等风险，生态环境部华北核与辐射安全监督站(以下简称华北监督站)压紧压实营运单位防汛防台主体责任，紧盯台风防御全过程，全力守护田湾核电站安全稳定运行，确保群众清凉平安度夏。
华北监督站始终坚守“宁可十防九空，不可万一失防”的底线思维，坚持提前谋划、紧盯关键，严格落实24小时应急值守制度。台风来临期间，现场监督员重点检查了田湾核电站应急值班人员、应急物资的准备情况，并对厂区排水管网、厂区重要构筑物等关键设施进行巡查，持续督促营运单位严格执行自然灾害应急预案，落实各项防汛措施，确保核设施纵深防御体系有效运转。同时，密切关注台风动态和气象预警信息，做到风险早发现、早预警、早处置。

title: 金七门核电2号机组常规岛第一罐混凝土浇筑启动
content:
2026-08-20 08:33 来源：中核浙能
8月18日22时16分，浙江金七门核电建设再迎关键节点，2号机组常规岛汽轮发电机厂房筏基底板第一罐混凝土浇筑(FCD)正式启动，标志着金七门核电2号机组常规岛主体工程全面开工，项目建设正式迈入土建施工新阶段。
此次浇筑的筏基底板作为常规岛核心承重结构，属于变截面超大体积防水抗渗特种混凝土结构，是常规岛筏板基础结构中体量最大、工况最关键、精度要求最高的核心板块。此次施工连续作业时间长、温控防裂要求高、施工组织难度大，为确保工程安全高质量完成，中核浙能充分发扬“主人翁”精神、发挥“主心骨”作用、担当“主力军”责任，联合施工单位、监理单位组建专项技术攻坚小组，立足1号常规岛FCD成熟施工经验，全面优化2号常规岛筏板施工流程，严格遵循核电建设最高质量标准与安全规范。
各参建单位提前统筹、精密部署，优化场内罐车循环运输路线，划分多泵点分区浇筑作业面;制定降雨、停电、设备故障等多套应急处置方案，开展全员专项安全技术交底;搭建智能测温监测网络，设置里表温差、降温速率超标双重预警机制;分区搭配双规格振捣棒作业、复合保温保湿养护体系;配齐多班次党员带班轮值作业队伍，全程保障浇筑作业连续、平稳、有序推进。
浇筑期间，全程现场巡查，严控安全质量风险;党员突击队、青年突击队坚守关键工序，发现问题即查即改;后勤团队同步做好餐饮、防暑降温及夜间照明等保障工作。项目全体建设者协同作战、压紧压实岗位责任，确保工程高质量完成。
下一步，中核浙能将继续秉持“安全是核工业的生命线”“建设期的质量就是运行期的核安全”理念，落实“绝对责任，最高标准，体系运行，经验反馈”要求，将“四个严格”行为文化落实到一线班组，积极践行“四个最优”卓越绩效理念，着力提升项目全体参建者的积极性、主动性、创造性，全力打造“安全、科技、经济、数字、廉洁”新质华龙示范工程。

content:
高温超导强场磁体夏季技术研讨会在上海成功召开
2026-08-20 08:35 来源：中国聚变能源有限公司 核聚变
8月19日，高温超导强场磁体夏季技术研讨会在中国聚变上海总部成功召开。中国聚变党委副书记、副总经理于雪峰，聚变工程设计所副所长薛雷出席会议。薛雷代表聚变工程设计所致辞，对与会专家的莅临指导表示热烈欢迎。会议由聚变工程设计所高温超导磁体研发部主任胡新波主持。
本次研讨会邀请到中科院理化技术研究所、中科院上海高等研究院、中科院合肥物质研究院强磁场科学中心、中山先进低温技术研究院、核工业西南物理研究院等科研院所，上海交通大学 、复旦大学、兰州大学、上海科技大学等高校，以及能量奇点、上海超导、东部超导、强场科技、辰光医疗、辰昊超导、中车时代电气等企业，共16家单位、26位行业专家参加。
会议集中展示了高温超导磁体技术阶段性研发成果，与会专家针对技术研发的难点开展了深入研讨，并提出了诸多有价值的建设性意见和建议，进一步深化了认识，凝聚了共识，为长三角高温超导磁体技术创新联合体的务实合作与成果落地注入了新动力，对高温超导强场磁体技术创新和产业高质量发展具有重要意义。
中国聚变科技与数字化部、聚变工程设计所有关负责同志和科研骨干参加会议。

title: Energy Fuels犹他州工厂氧化铽通过日本稀土永磁体制造商认证
content:
Energy Fuels犹他州工厂氧化铽通过日本稀土永磁体制造商认证
8月19日，美国关键材料生产商Energy Fuels Inc.宣布，其在犹他州White Mesa工厂生产的氧化铽已通过一家日本稀土永磁体制造商的全部认证，可用于商业化稀土永磁体生产，无需进一步资格认证或验证。
据公司介绍，该日本制造商是中国以外全球较大的稀土永磁体制造商之一。Energy Fuels表示，此次氧化铽通过认证，表明其重稀土产品质量和稀土加工能力已获得下游用户认可。公司此前生产的钕镨氧化物和镝氧化物也已获得用于稀土永磁体制造的资格认证。
铽是重要重稀土元素之一，主要用于提升高强度钕铁硼永磁体的耐热性和性能。钕铁硼永磁体广泛用于汽车、先进电子产品、机器人、航空航天等领域。根据Benchmark Mineral Intelligence的欧洲到岸价格数据，氧化铽目前市场价格约为每吨550万美元。
Energy Fuels表示，在完成对澳大利亚战略材料公司和真空熔炼公司的收购后，公司预计将形成从矿山到稀土永磁体的垂直整合供应链。其White Mesa工厂生产的钕镨、铽和镝氧化物将成为相关供应链的重要组成部分。
Energy Fuels是一家总部位于美国科罗拉多州莱克伍德的关键材料公司，业务涉及铀、稀土元素、重矿砂、钒及医用同位素开发。该公司是美国天然铀精矿生产商，其铀产品用于核能发电;位于犹他州的White Mesa工厂是美国一座获得全面许可的常规铀矿厂，同时生产稀土产品，并正在评估医用同位素回收在新兴癌症疗法中的应用。

title: IsoEnergy与DISA完成交易，成立美国铀回收与生产公司DISA Uranium
content:
IsoEnergy与DISA完成交易，成立美国铀回收与生产公司DISA Uranium
8月19日，IsoEnergy Ltd.与DISA Technologies, Inc.宣布，双方已完成此前披露的交易，成立DISA Uranium Corporation。新公司定位为技术型美国铀企业，计划加强美国本土铀供应，并服务于对本土核燃料日益增长的需求。
根据最终协议，IsoEnergy将其位于美国犹他州、已获许可且曾投产的传统铀矿资产组合转让给DISA Uranium，以换取DISA Uranium的1,677,350股普通股。该资产组合包括Tony M矿、Daneros矿、Rim矿、Sage Plain项目和Flatiron项目。交易完成后，DISA Uranium将整合IsoEnergy的犹他州铀矿资产、DISA的专有高效酸洗脱(HPSA™)技术，以及相关修复和回收业务。
同日，DISA Uranium还完成了此前宣布的1.05亿美元私募融资。参与方包括Tembo Capital、BHP Ventures、Galvanize Climate Solutions、Valor Equity Partners、Evok Innovations、Halliburton Labs和Veriten。IsoEnergy在该轮融资中投资3300万美元。交易和融资完成后，IsoEnergy持有DISA Uranium约33%的完全稀释后股份，成为其最大股东。
IsoEnergy首席执行官兼董事Philip Williams表示，交易完成释放了公司犹他州资产组合的价值，也使IsoEnergy能够参与美国铀矿平台的发展。DISA Uranium首席执行官Greyson Buckingham表示，公司将依托铀矿资产、技术和资金支持推进战略。
交易完成后，DISA Uranium董事会由7名董事组成，包括IsoEnergy董事会主席Richard Patricio、IsoEnergy首席执行官兼董事Phillip Williams、Tembo Capital合伙人George Pyper，以及DISA董事会现任成员Greyson Buckingham、Scott Saxberg、Marty Reed和前美国核管理委员会委员Jeffrey Merrifield。
按照计划，DISA Uranium将推进多线并行战略，重点包括利用高效酸洗脱(HPSA)技术从废弃矿山废料中回收铀，恢复美国传统铀矿生产，并发展本土加工能力。其中，Tony M矿预计将成为犹他州项目组合近期推进的重点，同时配合公司修复活动和更广泛的发展战略。
DISA Uranium总部位于美国怀俄明州卡斯珀市，业务包括从废弃铀矿废料中回收铀和钒，并修复美国西部遗留矿场。公司称，其持有美国核管理委员会颁发的相关许可证，可在多个矿场处理和回收废弃铀矿废料。IsoEnergy则是一家多元化铀矿公司，在加拿大、美国和澳大利亚等铀矿产区拥有处于不同开发阶段的矿产资源。

title: Mellifluous Fusion与Advaiya Solutions达成合作，面向聚变能源行业提供AI和商业技术方案
content:
Mellifluous Fusion与Advaiya Solutions达成合作，面向聚变能源行业提供AI和商业技术方案
8月19日，聚变能源营销公司美利弗卢斯聚变 (Mellifluous Fusion) 与商业技术公司阿德瓦亚解决方案公司 (Advaiya Solutions) 签署合作协议，双方将面向快速发展的聚变能源行业，提供业务应用、人工智能开发及部署等相关解决方案。
根据协议，双方合作重点包括通过集成化系统和人工智能工具，提升聚变能源供应链的运行效率、组织协同能力和响应速度。随着聚变能源相关企业、供应商和配套服务体系加快扩展，数字化业务系统和人工智能应用被视为支撑行业规模化发展的重要环节。
阿德瓦亚解决方案公司总裁达尔梅什·戈达 (Dharmesh Godha) 表示，随着聚变能源产业逐步发展，并有望成为能源和工业基础设施的重要组成部分，供应链效率、组织赋能和业务推进速度将变得更加关键。他说，Advaiya将利用成熟技术平台和集成应用，帮助复杂组织提升精简化、高效化和灵活性。
资料显示，阿德瓦亚解决方案公司是微软 (Microsoft)、Snowflake、OnePlan、Monday.com、Databricks和Sitecore等企业的优选合作伙伴，主要为企业提供工作运营、客户互动和数据利用等领域的数字化解决方案。
美利弗卢斯聚变首席执行官帕拉斯·沙阿 (Paras Shah) 表示，该公司以行业叙事和战略传播为核心，而聚变能源行业的发展叙事正越来越多地与技术、人工智能驱动增长、规模化部署和创新相关。与Advaiya合作，将有助于其围绕聚变能源商业化进程开展相关传播和协作。
Mellifluous Fusion方面称，聚变能源被认为有潜力为全球提供丰富、清洁的基础负荷能源。随着科技社会用能需求上升，以及人工智能等新兴应用快速发展，聚变能源商业化受到更多关注。不过，从技术突破走向大规模商业应用，聚变能源行业仍需在工程化、产业链建设和商业部署等方面继续推进。

title: West Engineering向阿库尤核电站2号机组交付30面继电保护与自动化柜
content:
West Engineering向阿库尤核电站2号机组交付30面继电保护与自动化柜
西部工程公司 (West Engineering) 已完成土耳其阿库尤核电站2号机组下一阶段设备交付，向项目现场运送30面继电保护与自动化柜。相关设备将用于动力装置关键电气元件的保护、监测和控制。
本次交付设备包括用于生成模拟量和离散量信息的AZ-PZ机柜、电源单元保护装置柜、功率单元测量装置柜、同步继电器柜、发电机开关控制柜、电气过程记录柜以及控制电流分配柜等。
据介绍，该批核设施用设备在设计中考虑了较高的安全裕度和容错能力。所供继电保护与自动化系统符合相关国际标准，安全等级为3H/N，符合NP-001-15标准;质量保证类别为QA3，设备从材料和部件选择到验收试验，均经过多阶段质量控制。
该批设备还可集成至西部工程公司自主研发的电气设备监控系统 (EEMCS)。通过统一平台，相关系统可实现保护、控制和测量装置的协调运行，集中收集和处理技术信息，并简化设备运行维护流程。同时，一体化集成有助于减少不同子系统之间的接口方案数量，提高动力装置电气部分的整体可靠性。
此次交付是阿库尤核电站四台机组设备供应合同的一部分。此前，西部工程公司已向该项目1号机组交付一套同类设备，同样包括30面继电保护与自动化柜。

title: 乌克兰批准扩建布里亚基夫卡放射性废物处置设施

乌克兰批准扩建布里亚基夫卡放射性废物处置设施
乌克兰国家核监管监察局 (SNRIU) 已批准在布里亚基夫卡放射性废物处置设施所在地建设一座新的处置库，用于处置切尔诺贝利核事故清理工作中产生的低放射性和中放射性废物。
布里亚基夫卡放射性废物处置设施位于切尔诺贝利禁区内，是乌克兰管理切尔诺贝利事故相关放射性废物的重要设施之一。该设施作为事故后优先应急措施的一部分建设，于1987年投入使用，主要接收来自切尔诺贝利地区的低放射性和中放射性废物。目前，该设施由乌克兰中央放射性废物管理企业 (CERWM) 运营。
截至目前，布里亚基夫卡设施已填满31个地面沟槽式处置单元。每个处置单元尺寸为150米×50米，主要工程屏障为厚度1米的特制黏土屏蔽层。最后一个投入使用的21A号处置库于2018年开始运行，并于2023年底完全填满。自投运以来，该设施累计处置约635918立方米切尔诺贝利相关放射性废物。
除常规废物外，切尔诺贝利事故处置过程中使用过的放射性污染车辆也存放在布里亚基夫卡设施内。CERWM自2012年起开始对这些车辆进行拆解和减容处理。
为扩大处置能力，CERWM计划新建11A号沟槽式处置库。该企业已完成并确认处置库施工设计，设计方案纳入了国家层面对项目进行综合专家审查后的意见。今年早些时候，CERWM向监管机构提交了在新处置库建设阶段开展相关活动的许可证申请。
SNRIU在国家核与辐射安全科学技术中心 (SSTC NRS) 参与下，对11A号处置库建设阶段安全分析报告进行了核与辐射安全方面的国家审查，重点评估项目是否符合相关法律、标准和监管要求。
在本周二举行的会议上，SNRIU董事会审议并批准了国家专家审查结论。审查结果确认，项目采用的设计决策具备合理性，拟建处置库满足安全要求，CERWM具备按照既定核与辐射安全标准及法规开展建设阶段活动的能力。
监管机构同时建议，CERWM在处置库建设阶段继续更新安全论证，并结合设计方案实际实施情况、设施特性变化以及放射性废物流情况，将相关内容纳入运行阶段安全分析报告和其他运行文件中，以便后续申请处置库运行阶段许可证。
SNRIU表示，新建近地表处置库建成并投入使用后，将有助于继续处置切尔诺贝利核电站退役过程中产生的低放射性废物，以及乌克兰其他核能领域相关单位产生的低放射性废物。

title: 印度与德国黑森州探讨清洁能源合作，议题涉及激光核聚变研究
content:
印度与德国黑森州探讨清洁能源合作，议题涉及激光核聚变研究
8月19日，印度商业和工业部长皮尤什·戈亚尔 (Piyush Goyal) 与德国黑森州 (Hesse) 州长鲍里斯·莱茵 (Boris Rhein) 举行会谈，双方就加强印度与黑森州之间的经济和技术合作进行讨论。德国联邦和欧洲事务、国际事务及去官僚化部长曼弗雷德·彭茨 (Manfred Pentz) 以及德国企业代表团出席会议。
会谈涉及多个新兴和高增长领域，其中与能源相关的内容集中在清洁能源和未来技术方向。双方讨论了黑森州在下一代能源技术方面的举措，包括基于激光的核聚变研究。相关内容被列为双方潜在合作领域之一。
戈亚尔表示，印度与黑森州企业在贸易、投资、技术和创新等方面具备进一步合作空间，尤其是在技术密集型和知识驱动型产业领域。黑森州方面则依托其工业基础、研发能力和技术生态，为相关合作提供支撑。
此次会谈还以印度—欧盟自由贸易协定为背景。双方认为，该协定有望改善市场准入，并为印度和欧盟企业之间的贸易、投资及技术合作创造新的机会。对于清洁能源和核聚变等前沿技术领域，双方将继续探索企业合作、技术伙伴关系和创新驱动增长的可能性。

title: 埃及计划在埃尔达巴核电站增建两台机组
content:
俄罗斯国家原子能公司
VVER-1200
埃及正计划在该国地中海沿岸的达巴核电站增建两台核电机组。目前，俄罗斯国家原子能公司 (Rosatom) 为该项目提供的4台机组已在建设中。
埃及电力和可再生能源部长马哈茂德·埃斯马特 (Mahmoud Esmat) 表示，相关扩建计划将与Rosatom进行讨论。埃及方面的消息称，目前谈判尚未设定时间表，扩建方案也尚未作出最终决定。
该扩建设想是埃及提升核能和可再生能源发电比重、降低传统燃料依赖的一部分。埃及尤其希望减少对天然气的依赖。美国能源信息署 (EIA) 数据显示，埃及化石燃料发电中超过80%依靠天然气，居民供气也大量依赖天然气。近年来，国内需求快速增长并超过本土产量，使埃及转为天然气净进口国，同时推动新的海上勘探和进口协议。
达巴核电站位于埃及马特鲁省，距开罗西北约300公里，是埃及首座核电站。Rosatom正在为该站建设4台三代+ VVER-1200压水堆机组，每台机组电功率为1200兆瓦。
根据国际原子能机构 (IAEA) 信息，达巴1号机组于2022年7月开工建设，2号机组于2022年11月开工，3号机组于2023年5月开工，4号机组于2024年1月开工。

title: 多瑙河水位回升 保克什核电站预计恢复满负荷运行
content:
多瑙河水位回升 保克什核电站预计恢复满负荷运行
匈牙利方面8月19日消息，彼得·马扎尔 (Peter Magyar) 表示，受多瑙河水位回升影响，保克什核电站 (Paks Nuclear Power Plant) 预计将于下周末恢复满负荷运行。
马扎尔称，自8月28日下周五起，保克什核电站将具备满负荷运行条件。近期多瑙河水位上涨15至20厘米，为电站恢复出力创造了条件，也使运营方无需再次停运汽轮机。相关专家计划尽快重启尚未恢复运行的汽轮机。
此前，由于多瑙河水位处于历史低位，依靠河水冷却的保克什核电站运行受到影响，电站出力一度降至满负荷约10%的水平。
